findings.paper_title: 7.1 - Edinburgh Visitor Levy Cultural Programming Fund Update
findings.headline: 5% of Visitor Levy collected in first three years ring-fenced as reserve to manage income volatility.
findings.detail: The council has agreed to set aside 5% of the levy collected across the first three years in a dedicated ring-fenced reserve, designed to smooth annual income fluctuations and provide buffer against visitor behaviour changes.
findings.matters: Demonstrates proactive financial management of a new, volatile revenue stream; shows the council is factoring revenue unpredictability into its funding model.
findings.figures: Reserve allocation: 5% of first three years' levy collection.
findings.quote: 5% of the levy collected in the first three years will be set aside in a ring-fenced reserve so that income volatility between years can be managed;

findings.paper_title: 7.1 - Edinburgh Visitor Levy Cultural Programming Fund Update
findings.headline: Income review scheduled December 2026; revenue shortfall may trigger project pause or allocation reduction.
findings.detail: Council will conduct an income review in December 2026 to compare actual levy revenue against projections. Should actual income fall below forecast, the council will determine whether to pause projects or reduce financial allocation for the remainder of the financial year. Projects are being programmed on a quarterly basis in preparation for this review.
findings.matters: This is a specific risk trigger point that could materially change the council's cultural programming spending within the first year; signals cash flow uncertainty and shows structured contingency management.
findings.figures: Review date: December 2026. Year 1 programming: quarterly basis.
findings.quote: Should the actual income be lower than projected, a review will be undertaken of the remaining planned expenditure of the financial year to determine whether there is the requirement to pause projects or reduce the financial allocation;

findings.paper_title: 7.1 - Edinburgh Visitor Levy Cultural Programming Fund Update
findings.headline: Cultural Programming Fund allocation £500k–£550k over three years from forecasted Visitor Levy income of £5.74m–£10.91m; council identifies visitor behaviour risk to revenue.
findings.detail: Council has allocated £500,000 (2026/27), £515,000 (2027/28), and £550,000 (2028/29) to cultural programming from the Culture Heritage and Events funding stream of the Visitor Levy. Underlying income is forecasted at £5.74m, £9.90m, and £10.91m respectively. The paper identifies that changes in visitor behaviour, including declining visitor numbers or shorter stays, may impact levy revenue.
findings.matters: Lenders and finance directors need to understand revenue volatility risks affecting council funding commitments; this scheme's income is explicitly dependent on visitor behaviour.
findings.quote: Changes in visitor behaviours (such as a decline in the number of visitors staying in Edinburgh and the number of nights they stay) may impact levy revenue.

findings.paper_title: 7.2 - Cultural Venues Fees and Charges
findings.headline: Late approval of Cultural Venues fees and charges creates in-year budget pressures due to long contracting lead times with hirers and promoters
findings.detail: The Council has identified that decisions on fees and charges made late in the financial year cannot be applied to existing contracts due to long lead times for venues' hirers and promoters. This creates in-year budget pressures in the subsequent year when income targets cannot be met. The Committee is recommending approval of fees at an earlier fixed point in each year to mitigate this planning constraint.
findings.matters: The timing of budget decisions affects the council's ability to hit income targets and manage financial planning; resolving service-specific operational constraints improves forecast reliability.
findings.figures: March 2026 Finance and Resources Committee approved 10% increase to Cultural Venues fees for 2026/27, equating to 'an additional income target of £180,000'
findings.quote: Decisions made on fees and charges late in the financial year are creating budget pressures within services in the subsequent year, as it is often too late to apply them due to contracting and supply chain lead times.

findings.paper_title: 7.2 - Cultural Venues Fees and Charges
findings.headline: Usher Hall performed ahead of target in 2025/6, enabling the Cultural Venues service to deliver a balanced budget
findings.detail: The Usher Hall venue exceeded its income target in 2025/6, allowing the wider Cultural Venues service to present a balanced budget for the year. The venues' budgets are underpinned by income from venue rentals, ticketing commissions, bars and catering, totalling just over £4.7m against budgeted cost turnover.
findings.matters: The positive performance of a material income-generating service demonstrates financial viability and capability to generate required revenues; relevant to assessing the service's sustainability and recovery trajectory.
findings.figures: 2025/6 total income target 'just over £4.7 million, excluding gross ticket sales, 92% of total budgeted cost turnover'; Usher Hall performed 'ahead of target'
findings.quote: The Usher Hall performed ahead of target, allowing the wider service to present a balanced budget for the year.

findings.paper_title: 7.2 - Cultural Venues Fees and Charges
findings.headline: Cultural Venues fees and charges to increase by 3% for 2027/28 and thereafter by CPI rate, moderating growth expectations from the baseline 5% annual assumption
findings.detail: The Committee is recommending a 3% increase in Cultural Venues fees and charges for 2027/28, with future years' increases set at the CPI rate from the preceding June. This represents a reduction from the baseline 5% annual increase currently assumed in the Council's medium-term financial plan. The Council acknowledges this 'may result in a shortfall relative to these baseline assumptions' but expects the certainty of early fee-setting to maintain bookings and competitive position.
findings.matters: The decision moderates income growth expectations for a £4.7m revenue service, which has direct implications for the 2027/28 budget and MTFP; the trade-off between lower income growth and planning certainty affects financial delivery.
findings.figures: 3% increase for 2027/28; baseline assumption 5%; 2025/6 income target 'just over £4.7 million, excluding gross ticket sales, 92% of total budgeted cost turnover'
findings.quote: Whilst the setting of the 2027/28 increase at 3%, and subsequent years' at the level of inflation at June of the preceding year, may result in a shortfall relative to these baseline assumptions, the certainty of future fees and charges is expected to maintain current overall bookings

findings.paper_title: 8.2 - Culture and Communities Committee Revenue Budget Monitoring 202627 – Month Three position
findings.headline: Edinburgh Leisure contingency of £1.868m provided in 2025/26 assumed not required for 2026/27
findings.detail: The council provided up to £1.868m of additional in-year support to Edinburgh Leisure in 2025/26 to address savings shortfalls. The 2026/27 approved budget assumes this additional funding is not required this year, pending implementation of recurring measures within Edinburgh Leisure.
findings.matters: This is a material contingency: if Edinburgh Leisure's financial position deteriorates and this support is required again, it would add £1.868m to the council's pressures in 2026/27. The budget relies on this assumption holding.
findings.figures: £1.868m (2025/26 support); assumed £0 for 2026/27
findings.quote: At the meeting of City of Edinburgh Council on 18 December 2025, Council approved the provision of up to £1.868m of additional in-year support to Edinburgh Leisure... The 2026/27 approved budget and month three forecast is based on this additional funding not being required this year

findings.matters: Indicates that actual service demand or utilisation patterns differ from what was budgeted, a leading indicator of potential demand-side stress across the service portfolio.

findings.quote: The service is forecasting to have a net overspend of £0.052m arising from income being lower than budgeted levels due to changes in demand and service utilisation, and increased costs of provision

findings.paper_title: 8.2 - Culture and Communities Committee Revenue Budget Monitoring 202627 – Month Three position
findings.headline: Parks and Greenspaces £0.203m overspend from additional transport charges and temporary toilet facility costs
findings.detail: This service is forecasting a £0.203m overspend on its £7.706m budget driven by increases in transport charges and the cost of providing temporary toilet facilities. These are operating cost pressures rather than demand or income related.
findings.matters: Shows sustained cost inflation in operational areas (transport costs) and reveals unplanned costs (temporary facilities) that were not absorbed within budget.
findings.figures: £0.203m overspend on £7.706m budget
findings.quote: The service is forecasting expenditure to be £0.203m more than budget for 2026/27, reflecting additional transport charges and the cost of temporary toilet facilities

findings.headline: Heritage, Cultural Venues and Museums £0.170m overspend from premises costs, retail services, and monument maintenance pressures
findings.detail: The £0.170m forecast overspend in this service comprises additional premises costs of £0.020m, a net pressure of £0.125m for retail services, and a net pressure of £0.135m on the Scott and Nelson monuments. findings.matters: Shows that these services are not in budget balance at month three and indicates where within the council the overspend is concentrated.
findings.figures: £0.425m total; £0.170m Culture and Wellbeing, £0.203m Parks and Greenspaces, £0.052m Bereavement Services

findings.paper_title: 8.2 - Culture and Communities Committee Revenue Budget Monitoring 202627 – Month Three position
findings.headline: Failure to break even in 2026/27 will require reinstatement of General Fund unallocated reserve in 2027/28, increasing future savings requirements
findings.detail: The paper explicitly flags that if the council does not achieve break-even by year-end, it will need to rebuild the General Fund unallocated reserve in 2027/28. This mechanism converts a one-year overspend into a multi-year structural problem, requiring larger savings targets in future years.
findings.matters: This structural dynamic means the problem compounds year-on-year; a finance director needs to understand this is not a one-off pressure but will create elevated savings requirements going forward.
findings.figures: Not quantified separately; impacts 2027/28 savings requirement
findings.quote: Failure to break even in 2026/27 may increase the savings requirement in 2027/28 due to a need to reinstate the General Fund unallocated reserve

findings.headline: General Fund revenue budget overspend of £8.615m forecast at month three
findings.detail: The council-wide position, reported to Finance and Resources Committee on 24 September, shows a projected overall overspend of £8.615m at month three. This represents the position across all services and is material to the council's financial position for the year.
findings.matters: A council-wide deficit of this magnitude at month three signals sustained financial pressure that will require significant corrective action and may impact reserve deployment.
findings.quote: an overall overspend of £8.615m is projected

findings.detail: The audit identified an increase in demand for temporary accommodation (Paragraph 47) and recorded a significant finding on accounting for temporary accommodation changes. This represents demand-driven costs the council cannot readily control.

findings.detail: The audit's wider scope assessment (Exhibit 7) flagged significant risks specifically in long-term borrowing and funding. The committee decision explicitly highlights this finding, indicating it is a material concern distinct from the clean opinion on the accounts themselves.

findings.paper_title: The City of Edinburgh Council - 2025-26 Annual Audit Report - Referral from the Governance, Risk and Best Value Committee
findings.headline: Council plans to double debt while HRA debt servicing reaches 63% of income by 2030/31
findings.detail: The committee decision explicitly notes the council's proposed doubling of debt alongside projected HRA debt servicing rising to 63% of income by 2030/31. The committee states these matters, taken together with auditor concerns about borrowing and funding gaps, should be taken seriously, signalling high concern about whether debt levels are sustainable.
findings.matters: A doubling of debt with HRA debt service at 63% of income represents severe leverage that constrains financial flexibility and raises acute affordability concerns for any lender considering exposure to this council.
findings.figures: "proposed doubling of the Council's debt"; HRA debt servicing at "63% by 2030/31"
findings.quote: the proposed doubling of the Council's debt, the increase in percentage of Housing Revenue Account income to be spent on debt servicing to 63% by 2030/31 and the likely increase in cost of debt

findings.paper_title: Treasury Management Annual Report 2025-26
findings.headline: Most new borrowing was taken at the shorter end of the yield curve to lock in rates below budget, creating medium-term refinancing risk.
findings.detail: The council deliberately took most 2025/26 borrowing at shorter maturities to achieve rates below budget while longer-term rates remained at near 30-year highs. This trade-off creates a maturity wall of short-dated debt requiring refinancing in future years, potentially at higher costs.
findings.matters: Short-dated borrowing concentrates refinancing risk. With the council's large forward borrowing needs and elevated gilt yields, this creates vulnerability to future rate movements.
findings.figures: £350m borrowed from PWLB at 4.60% average; most taken at shorter end of yield curve
findings.quote: Most of the borrowing undertaken was at the shorter end of the yield curve. While this has created some additional medium-term re-financing risk, it has allowed the borrowing to be taken at rates below that budgeted for.

findings.paper_title: Treasury Management Annual Report 2025-26
findings.headline: Treasury cash fund generated £14.5m additional income to the council by outperforming its investment benchmark.
findings.detail: The Treasury Cash Fund delivered 4.18% average return against a benchmark of 3.96%, and 4.69% rate at year-end against benchmark 3.67%. Outperformance was achieved through strategic placement of fixed-rate deposits with other local authorities. This provides partial offset to rising debt costs.
findings.matters: Investment income of £14.5m is material against total debt costs of £86.2m. However, this depends on maintained cash holdings and market conditions—not a sustainable funding source as borrowing programme expands.
findings.figures: £14.5m income generated; average rate 4.18% vs benchmark 3.96%; closing rate 4.69% vs benchmark 3.67%
findings.quote: The fund generated income of £14.5m during 2025/26 to CEC and the Cash Fund interest rate at 31 March 2026 was 4.69% against a benchmark of 3.67%.

findings.paper_title: Treasury Management Annual Report 2025-26
findings.headline: Council repaid two LOBO loans at par when lenders exercised their call options, in a refinancing and liquidity event.
findings.detail: Two Lender Option Borrower Option loans were included in the £32m of market debt repaid during 2025/26. When lenders exercised their options to request higher rates, the council exercised its option to repay at par. The remaining LOBO portfolio of £122.4m remains outstanding, with maturities from 2028 to 2066 and interest rates from 4.375% to 5.25%.
findings.matters: LOBO calls represent refinancing events requiring immediate cash and replacement funding at potentially higher rates. With rates elevated, remaining £122m of LOBO exposure creates ongoing call risk.
findings.figures: £32m market debt repaid (including two LOBOs); outstanding LOBO debt £122.4m
findings.quote: The lenders exercised their option to request an increase in the interest rate paid on the loans and the Council exercised its option to repay the loans at par with no penalty.

findings.paper_title: Treasury Management Annual Report 2025-26
findings.headline: HRA financing ratio rising from 39.2% in 2025/26 to 64.6% by 2030/31; General Services ratio rising from 7.5% to 10.9%
findings.detail: Prudential Indicator 2 shows General Services financing ratio rising from 7.5% to 10.9% over six years, while HRA ratio rises from 39.2% to 64.6%. By 2030/31, rental income will be almost entirely committed to debt service, leaving little financial flexibility.
findings.matters: High financing ratios constrain the council's capacity to respond to cost pressures, service demands, or revenue shortfalls, and raise questions about the long-term sustainability of the housing programme.
findings.figures: HRA financing ratio: 39.2% (2025/26) → 64.6% (2030/31); General Services: 7.5% → 10.9%
findings.quote: Ratio of Financing Costs to Net Revenue Stream...Housing Revenue Account (HRA) 39.2%...64.6% [through 2030/31]

findings.paper_title: Treasury Management Annual Report 2025-26
findings.headline: Capital Financing Requirement will nearly double from £2.8bn to £5.7bn by 2030/31, driven by housing and school investment following declared housing emergency.
findings.detail: Prudential Indicator 3 shows CFR growing from £2,795.9m in 2025/26 to £5,677.4m in 2030/31. General Services CFR rises from £2,026m to £3,175m and HRA CFR rises from £635m to £2,304m, reflecting the council's capital commitments to housing and school infrastructure.
findings.matters: This debt trajectory directly determines the council's borrowing requirement and debt servicing burden over the medium term. The pace of accumulation creates refinancing risk if market conditions deteriorate.
findings.quote: Total Capital Financing Requirement £2,795.9m...£5,677.4m [for years 2025/26 through 2030/31]

findings.paper_title: Treasury Management Annual Report 2025-26
findings.headline: Council explicitly warns it is running significant financing risk due to large future borrowing needs while long-term rates remain at nearly 30-year highs.
findings.detail: The paper warns that with the large capital expenditure programme ahead, the council faces significant financing risk. Most 2025/26 borrowing was taken at the shorter end of the yield curve to lock in rates below budget, creating medium-term refinancing risk, while longer-term rates remain exceptionally high.
findings.matters: This is an explicit risk acknowledgement from the council itself about its ability to refinance on acceptable terms as short-dated debt matures. Rate risk management becomes critical to financial sustainability.
findings.figures: 10-year gilt yield: 4.65% opening to 4.86% closing (high 4.95%, low 4.23%); PWLB borrowing at 4.60% average
findings.quote: With the large value of borrowing required over the next few years to fund the capital expenditure programme, the Council is running a significant financing risk at present.

findings.paper_title: Treasury Management Annual Report 2025-26
findings.headline: Interest costs on borrowing increased by 14.9% in one year, from £77.6m to £86.2m, as new lending was taken at higher rates.
findings.detail: External interest cost component increased from £67.2m to £77.5m. This reflects the council borrowing £350m from PWLB at 4.60% average and £15m from another local authority at 4.15% during 2025/26, at a time when PWLB rates were elevated and volatile.
findings.matters: Rising debt servicing costs reduce financial headroom, and the trajectory is set to worsen significantly over the next six years as capital commitments require additional borrowing.
findings.figures: £86.2m in 2025/26 vs £77.6m in 2024/25; external component £77.5m vs £67.2m
findings.quote: The cost of debt increased from £77.6m in 2024/25 to £86.2m in 2025/26. The external interest cost component of that increased from £67.2m to £77.5m, reflecting the significant level of new borrowing at higher interest rates.

findings.paper_title: Capital Monitoring and Revised Budget M3
findings.headline: Coatfield Lane housing project experiencing escalating costs and planning-driven redesign, £3.4m reprofiled
findings.detail: The Coatfield Lane project has experienced cost escalation and required redesign. An additional planning requirement for sub-station relocation (following discussion with SPEN, the electricity network operator) has been added, resulting in £3.4m being pushed back from 2026-27. Scope appears to be expanding rather than slipping temporally.
findings.matters: Cost escalation combined with unplanned scope addition (sub-station relocation) signals project risk and indicates utility coordination complexity. The scale suggests this may be a larger project than the reprofiling amount suggests.
findings.figures: £3.4m pushed back to 2026-27
findings.quote: Coatfield Lane has seen delays due to escalating costs and therefore a requirement for redesign. There has also been an additional planning permission requirement for a sub-station relocation following discussions with SPEN. This has led to £3.4m being pushed back to 2026-27.

findings.paper_title: Capital Monitoring and Revised Budget M3
findings.headline: General Fund capital programme requires £735.5m total borrowing cost (£254.4m principal + £481.1m interest) at 5.25% over 50 years
findings.detail: The revised 2026-27 General Fund capital budget carries borrowing charges of £735.5m in principal and interest. This is charged at an assumed rate of 5.25% and amortised over 50 years, resulting in average annual repayment of £14.7m. HRA carries additional £333.5m total cost (£115.4m principal + £218.2m interest).
findings.matters: Shows scale of the council's capital borrowing commitment and debt service cost. The 50-year amortisation and 5.25% rate assumption are material to revenue forecasts. Together General Fund and HRA total £1.07bn in borrowing cost.
findings.figures: General Fund: £254.4m principal, £481.1m interest, £735.5m total, average £14.7m/year over 50 years at 5.25%. HRA: £115.4m principal, £218.2m interest, £333.5m total, average £6.7m/year
findings.quote: The estimated loans charges associated with the revised 2026-27 General Fund budget amount to a principal repayment of £254.4m and interest of £481.1m. This would be a total cost of £735.5m with an average annual repayment of £14.7m over 50 years, based on an assumed loans fund interest rate of 5.25%.

findings.paper_title: Capital Monitoring and Revised Budget M3
findings.headline: MacMillan Hub project incurred £1.6m overspend from unforeseen building conditions, cost recovery from partner outstanding
findings.detail: The MacMillan Hub has exceeded budget by £1.6m due to unforeseen building conditions discovered during construction. Cost allocation between North Edinburgh Arts (the co-investor) and the council's library element has not yet been finalised. The council's net exposure depends on recovery from NEA.
findings.matters: Project overspend due to unforeseen conditions indicates either survey or procurement risk. Unresolved cost-split with a partner creates contingent liability and revenue uncertainty.
findings.figures: £1.6m overspend; allocation between NEA and council outstanding
findings.quote: the MacMillan Hub project has incurred an overspend (£1.6m) due to unforeseen building conditions. The final allocation of costs between the North Edinburgh Arts (NEA) and the Council's library element remains outstanding and the amount due from NEA will be detailed in a further report to Finance & Resources Committee in due course.

findings.paper_title: Capital Monitoring and Revised Budget M3
findings.headline: High-Rise residential retrofit programme experiencing delayed site starts, £46.3m reprofiled to future years
findings.detail: Two major retrofit programmes (Craigmillar/Peffermill and Cables Wynd/Linksview) have experienced delayed site commencement. The Cables Wynd/Linksview programme had to refocus its design phase on an early-works package to manage programme risk. Total reprofiling is £46.3m from 2026-27 to future years.
findings.matters: Largest single slippage in HRA capital programme. Delays in residential retrofit affect housing condition targets and may create maintenance liability. The requirement to pause design to manage early-works risk signals programme complexity.
findings.figures: £46.3m reprofiled to future years
findings.quote: The High-Rise Programme has seen delayed site starts for the Craigmillar/Peffermill and Cables Wynd/Linksview retrofit programmes and therefore £46.3 has been reprofiled into future years. The main design phase for Cables Wynd/Linksview had to refocus on an early works package to help de-risk the overall programme.

findings.paper_title: Capital Monitoring and Revised Budget M3
findings.headline: Primary and secondary school capital programme slipped significantly at design stage, £29.6m moved to future years
findings.detail: Fourteen primary and secondary school projects are in early design stages. New cost projections have moved £16m of primary school expenditure and £13.6m of secondary school expenditure from 2026-27 to future years. Granton Waterfront primary school is dependent on completion of site remediation works on the Granton Waterfront project, which itself has been reprofiled.
findings.matters: Design-stage delays cascade across multiple school projects. The dependency on Granton remediation completion creates sequencing risk. Slippage affects borrowing profile and revenue forecasts.
findings.figures: £16m primary schools, £13.6m secondary schools; total £29.6m reprofiled to future years
findings.quote: A number of the new primary schools in the programme are progressing through the early design stages and updated cost projections suggest £16m will occur in future years rather than 2026-27. A significant portion of this is for Granton Waterfront primary school which has a dependency on the land remediation works included within the Granton Waterfront Project.

findings.paper_title: Capital Monitoring and Revised Budget M3
findings.headline: Multi-Storey Services maintenance programme hit by failed tender for storage tank replacements, £6.4m slipped
findings.detail: A second-phase tender exercise for cold-water storage tank replacements failed, and the lift replacement programme has underperformed. This has resulted in £6.4m of programmed expenditure not now expected in 2026-27. This relates to maintenance of multi-storey residential buildings.
findings.matters: Failed procurement on HRA maintenance infrastructure signals supply chain difficulty and may indicate cost or capacity constraints in the housing repair market. Slippage affects HRA asset condition and maintenance backlog.
findings.figures: £6.4m not expected in 2026-27
findings.quote: The Multi-Storey Services investment programme is continuing to feel the impact of a failed tender exercise for the second phase of Cold-Water Storage Tank replacements and underperformance on the lift replacement programme, meaning £6.4m of expenditure is now not expected to occur in 2026-27.

findings.paper_title: Capital Monitoring and Revised Budget M3
findings.headline: Additional £32.4m Affordable Housing Grant from Scottish Government received, must be spent in 2026-27 or lost
findings.detail: Unexpected additional grant funding (total grant now £66.4m instead of budgeted £34m) has arrived for affordable housing. If allocated to HRA rather than registered social landlords, it would replace anticipated loans fund advances and reduce revenue budget through lower loan charges. This is time-critical – unspent funding will be clawed back.
findings.matters: New grant funding reduces borrowing requirement and revenue pressure if deployed to HRA. However, it creates a deadline-driven spending obligation and represents variability in grant funding assumptions – material to refinancing and revenue planning.
findings.figures: £32.4m additional grant (total now £66.4m vs £34m originally assumed); section 7.12 states £19m per year assumption but £66.4m available in 2026-27
findings.quote: an additional £32.4m is expected to be received in Affordable Housing Grant from the Scottish Government in 2026-27, over and above what was included in the original budget. This funding will support eligible affordable housing projects with qualifying expenditure within the current financial year and can be allocated to both HRA and to Registered Social Landlord (RSL) projects approved by Scottish Government. Should any of this be allocated to the HRA, this would replace anticipated loans fund advances and therefore save revenue budget by reducing loans charges.

findings.paper_title: Capital Monitoring and Revised Budget M3
findings.headline: Millerhill Energy from Waste contract signing delayed by Project Agreement negotiations; £7.9m budget increased and deferred beyond 2026/27
findings.detail: Ongoing negotiations to vary the Project Agreement have prevented the operator and preferred bidder from signing the design and build contract. The paper states the £7.9m budget allocation is now not likely to occur in 2026-27 and implies the figure will increase.
findings.matters: Delayed contract signature and cost pressure on a major energy infrastructure project affects capital expenditure profile and borrowing timing. Protracted negotiations suggest commercial risk or terms complexity.
findings.figures: £7.9m, stated to be "increased and is now not likely to occur in 2026-27"
findings.quote: protracted negotiations around agreeing a variation to the Project Agreement have delayed the signing of the design and build contract by the operator and the preferred bidder. This delay means the £7.9m is to be increased and is now not likely to occur in 2026-27.

findings.paper_title: Capital Monitoring and Revised Budget M3
findings.headline: Meadowbank housing development experiencing significant delay, cost agreement not yet reached with contractor
findings.detail: The council's largest HRA capital commitment is stalled at the cost agreement stage. £32.9m of site remediation and affordable housing construction was budgeted for 2026-27 but cannot proceed until cost terms are agreed. No timeline for resolution is stated.
findings.matters: A £32.9m project at cost-agreement deadlock signals potential structural issues in the council's ability to procure and execute major capital programmes. Delay pushes spending to future years and affects borrowing profile.
findings.figures: £32.9m, budgeted for 2026-27, now delayed
findings.quote: The Meadowbank development is experiencing a significant delay against the programme previously reported to committee. It was anticipated that £32.9m of site remediation works and affordable housing construction would occur in 2026-27, however an agreement on costs is yet to be reached with the contractor.

findings.paper_title: Capital Monitoring and Revised Budget M3
findings.headline: Fountainbridge development contractor withdrawn over risk-share terms, £13m delayed to future years
findings.detail: A development contractor withdrew from the Fountainbridge housing development agreement because standard terms were not agreed, specifically around risk allocation. The project is now progressing with a different supplier. This is one of several major housing projects experiencing supplier issues.
findings.matters: Contractor withdrawal affects delivery of housing supply within the emergency programme, delays major capital expenditure and borrowing drawdown, and may indicate procurement/commercial difficulties affecting the council's ability to execute its capital strategy.
findings.figures: £13.0m delayed to future years
findings.quote: For the Fountainbridge development, standard terms were not agreed with the contractor, specifically in relation to risk share, and they have withdrawn from the Development Agreement. The project is now progressing through another supplier, but this has led to the requirement to delay budget of £13.0m to future years.

findings.paper_title: 8.2 Revenue Monitoring M3
findings.headline: Homelessness Services showing £1.730m adverse variance against business case assumptions at month 3, being offset by drawing on risk contingency.
findings.detail: Slippage against homelessness business case assumptions created £1.730m adverse variance. Offset in full by drawing on risk contingency element approved as part of 2026/27 budget. Demand exceeding business case assumptions early in financial year.
findings.matters: Demand-led pressure in critical service materialising early and faster than anticipated; contingency is finite resource, so if trend continues through year could exhaust reserved funds.
findings.figures: £1.730m adverse variance; offset by risk contingency
findings.quote: an element of slippage against business case assumptions is contributing to an adverse variance for Homelessness Services of £1.730m, with this being offset in full by an element of the risk contingency approved as part of the 2026/27 budget.

findings.paper_title: 8.2 Revenue Monitoring M3
findings.headline: Edinburgh Integration Joint Board has £18.4m of approved health and social care savings that must be delivered, with council warning delivery and demand management are critical.
findings.detail: EIJB currently projects balanced position but paper flags £18.4m of approved savings as most material risk. Report notes delivery of review-linked savings and managing demand growth will be critical to maintaining budget balance through remainder of year. Spot purchasing pressures noted in direct payments, care at home, and residential/nursing care.
findings.matters: Large savings requirement in demand-led health and social care services, which are difficult to control; council explicitly flagged this as most material budget risk at budget-setting.
findings.figures: £18.4m of approved EIJB savings flagged as key risk; current month 3 position balanced but contingent on delivery
findings.quote: delivery of review-linked savings and managing demand growth will be critical in maintaining expenditure within budgeted levels for the remainder of the year

findings.paper_title: 8.2 Revenue Monitoring M3
findings.headline: Corporate Grip and Control approved savings of £1.9m has only delivered £0.55m by month 3, with £1.35m shortfall forecast.
findings.detail: £1.35m shortfall against approved corporate savings target of £1.9m. Work continuing to identify further opportunities. This is corporate-level, rather than service-specific, measure.
findings.matters: Significant corporate savings shortfall indicates difficulty in delivering even corporate-level cost controls, suggesting service-level savings risk is acute.
findings.figures: £0.55m of £1.9m delivered; £1.35m shortfall forecast
findings.quote: Relative to an approved total saving of £1.9m, £0.550m of savings have been identified to date.

findings.paper_title: 8.2 Revenue Monitoring M3
findings.headline: Property optimisation approved savings of £2.616m has only yielded £1.372m of identified savings by month 3, leaving £1.244m shortfall.
findings.detail: Property optimisation approved as savings measure. By month 3, only £1.372m identified through combination of Waverley Court rental income, depots review, energy savings and other measures. Remaining £1.244m shortfall being addressed through review of full property operational cost base, Best Value findings and rationalisation opportunities.
findings.matters: Material approved savings measure slipping; council has not yet identified more than half the savings it committed to deliver.
findings.figures: £1.372m of £2.616m identified; implied shortfall £1.244m
findings.quote: as of month three, through a combination of additional Waverley Court partner rental income, the depots review, energy savings and other Place-related grip and control savings, plans to deliver £1.372m of the approved saving of £2.616m have been developed.

findings.paper_title: 8.2 Revenue Monitoring M3
findings.headline: Scottish Government delayed parking Penalty Charge Notice fee increase to April 2028, deferring £1.05m of planned in-year income and extending budget pressure into 2027/28.
findings.detail: Council had included approved savings based on expected cumulative inflation-based increase to parking PCN fees. Scottish Government consultation delays implementation to April 2028, meaning no additional income until that date. Paper notes implications will require consideration in 2027/28 budget.
findings.matters: Planned income measure deferred due to external regulatory decision; creates immediate in-year shortfall and extends budget pressure into future years.
findings.figures: £1.05m shortfall; implementation deferred to April 2028
findings.quote: Although this is expected to result in the application of a cumulative inflation-based increase to current fees, this will not be introduced until April 2028, meaning that no additional income will be generated until that time.

findings.paper_title: 8.2 Revenue Monitoring M3
findings.headline: Parking income underperforming budget despite 2026/27 budget specifically designed to address prior year income pressure.
findings.detail: Approved parking income budget for 2026/27 addressed income pressure highlighted in 2025/26. However, actual income to date reduced in absolute terms compared to 2025/26, creating £0.7m shortfall against revised budget. Continuing downward trend despite budget response.
findings.matters: Shows key income stream deteriorating even after budget response; sustained weakness in material council income source.
findings.figures: £0.7m shortfall vs 2026/27 budget; income levels reduced in absolute terms vs 2025/26
findings.quote: parking income – the approved 2026/27 budget addressed, in full, the income pressure highlighted within the service in 2025/26. Income levels to date in 2026/27 have, however, reduced in absolute terms compared to the prior year and while the position will be kept under close review, a £0.7m shortfall relative to budget is forecast at this time

findings.paper_title: 8.2 Revenue Monitoring M3
findings.headline: Council Tax Premium for Second Homes and Long-Term Empty Properties implementation delayed to January 2027, creating £3m in-year income shortfall.
findings.detail: Approved income-raising measure delayed from planned implementation. Additionally, Council Tax base buoyancy reduced relative to 2025/26 outturn. Paper notes risk of recurring shortfall and will monitor through financial year.
findings.matters: Planned income source deferred; combined with reduced tax base buoyancy, signals potential structural income weakness beyond just timing.
findings.figures: £3m in-year shortfall; implementation date 1 January 2027
findings.quote: Following Council's approval of a revised implementation date of January 2027, a £3m in-year income shortfall is now being projected.

findings.paper_title: 8.2 Revenue Monitoring M3
findings.headline: Council considering using 2025/26 underspend to offset 2026/27 overspend; failure to break even may require reserve reinstatement in 2027/28
findings.detail: Paper states failure to break even in 2026/27 may require reinstatement of General Fund unallocated reserve in 2027/28, indicating existential risk to reserve position. Separately, paper recommends setting aside unallocated element of 2025/26 underspend to help balance current year, consuming prior year surplus to cover structural current-year overspend.
findings.matters: Suggests reserves depleted or at risk and council relying on one-off prior year funds to cover current year; this is unsustainable and indicates structural overspend.
findings.figures: £8.615m current year overspend; prior year underspend being drawn on
findings.quote: Failure to break even in 2026/27 may increase the savings requirement in 2027/28 due to a need to reinstate the General Fund unallocated reserve.

findings.paper_title: 8.2 Revenue Monitoring M3
findings.headline: Council forecasting £8.615m overspend at month 3 with 22% of approved savings delivery slipping against plan.
findings.detail: The 2026/27 budget was approved as balanced, dependent on delivery of £32.5m of approved savings. Month 3 monitoring shows an overall overspend of £8.615m (0.5% of net budget) with 78% of savings assessed as on track, implying 22% slipping. Paper emphasises urgent need for robust implementation plans or budget framework integrity will be compromised.
findings.matters: Shows material and immediate gap between approved budget and forecast out-turn; indicates that approved savings strategy is not delivering as planned and in-year management is falling short.
findings.figures: £8.615m overspend forecast; £32.5m of approved savings required for balanced budget; 78% of savings assessed on track; 0.5% of net budget
findings.quote: an overall overspend of £8.615m is being forecast... This position primarily reflects slippage in the delivery of approved savings, with 78% by value assessed to be on track at this stage

findings.paper_title: 7.3 Budget Strategy Update and MTFP
findings.headline: Pay award negotiations for 2027/28 have not yet begun, with council planning assumption of 3% for both teaching and non-teaching staff.
findings.detail: Current pay agreements run through March 2027 (teaching staff through July 2027). Officers have assumed 3% pay increases for future years based on recent settlement history and the Scottish Government Public Pay Policy, but actual negotiations have not yet started. Pay awards are a frequent source of budget pressure exceeding planning assumptions. Any settlement significantly above 3% would add directly to the £14.3m budget gap.
findings.matters: Pay settlements are a material cost driver and this assumption is still at-risk. The 3% figure is not yet locked in and represents a vulnerability in the projections.
findings.figures: 3% planning assumption (not yet negotiated)
findings.quote: As of the time of writing, negotiations on future years' pay awards are yet to begin, with a planning assumption, based on recent years' settlements and the broad Scottish Government Public Pay Policy 1, of 3% increases for both the teaching and non-teaching groups.

findings.paper_title: 7.3 Budget Strategy Update and MTFP
findings.headline: Scottish block grant funding faces provisional £728m reduction in 2027/28, creating uncertainty around how this will be distributed across councils.
findings.detail: The block grant reconciliation based on 2024/25 Scottish Income Tax collections points to a £728m reduction in block grant funding available to Scotland in 2027/28. This reduction exceeds Scottish Government's permitted borrowing and must be managed through its wider spending plans. Edinburgh's current MTFP assumes flat-cash core funding, but the outcome of Scottish Government's distribution decisions is uncertain. The settlement may also cover one or multiple years, adding to the uncertainty.
findings.matters: This creates material uncertainty about Edinburgh's funding baseline. While the council assumes flat-cash, a £728m national shortfall could result in reductions to local government funding that would materially worsen Edinburgh's position.
findings.figures: £728m reduction at Scottish level
findings.quote: The reconciliation points to a provisional £728 million reduction in the level of block grant funding available in 2027/28 and this reduction, which exceeds the Scottish Government's permitted borrowing as set out in the UK and Scottish Government's Fiscal Framework, will therefore require to be managed as part of its wider plans.

findings.paper_title: 7.3 Budget Strategy Update and MTFP
findings.headline: Homelessness and adult social care services flagged as areas with material risk around service demand in the 2027/28 budget.
findings.detail: The council has explicitly flagged risks around service demand in homelessness services and adult social care. The funding gap assumes these remain stable, but demand-led pressures in these areas require discretionary spending and could emerge quickly. If demand increases—particularly in homelessness, where need can spike—Edinburgh would face pressure to find additional funding on top of the £14.3m gap.
findings.matters: Homelessness and adult social care are discretionary services where demand shocks can create sudden budget pressures. These are specifically called out as risk areas by the council's finance team.
findings.figures: None quantified; risks flagged but not modeled
findings.quote: Risks also exist around service demand, particularly in Homelessness Services and Adult Social Care.

findings.paper_title: 7.3 Budget Strategy Update and MTFP
findings.headline: Lothian Pension Fund triennial valuation expected early 2027, with each 1% change in non-teaching employer contribution rates costing Edinburgh £4.1m.
findings.detail: The Lothian Pension Fund will conclude its triennial valuation in early 2027, determining employer pension contributions for the council's non-teaching workforce (and Council-delegated services within the Integration Joint Board) for 2027/28 to 2029/30. Each 1% change equates to £4.1m cost to Edinburgh. The outcome is currently unknown. Officers are discussing mitigation of this uncertainty, and a further update is expected in the November report. This timing means the valuation outcome will not be known until after major budget decisions must be taken.
findings.matters: Each 1% change represents several million pounds of cost or benefit and is material to the budget gap. The outcome is unknown and the timing of the valuation creates a gap between the decision-point and the resolution of this uncertainty.
findings.figures: £4.1m per 1% change; valuation outcome expected early 2027
findings.quote: Each 1% change in the employer's contribution rate, including Council-delegated services within the Edinburgh Integration Joint Boad, equates to a cost to the Council of £4.1m

findings.paper_title: 7.3 Budget Strategy Update and MTFP
findings.headline: Scotland-wide adult social care funding sustainability is being questioned, and Edinburgh has not assumed any increase in core contribution to its Integration Joint Board beyond pass-through.
findings.detail: The paper flags that the sustainability of current Scotland-wide adult social care funding levels without significant service reductions is being increasingly questioned. This is a systemic concern rather than a localized one. Meanwhile, Edinburgh's 2027/28 projections include no assumed increase in the council's core contribution to the Edinburgh Integration Joint Board beyond pass-through of sums from the Settlement. If Scotland-wide funding pressures result in calls for increased local contributions, Edinburgh would face additional unexpected cost pressure on top of the £14.3m gap.
findings.matters: Adult social care is typically a material and growing budget for councils. System-wide questioning of sustainability suggests this could become a problem area for Edinburgh's budget position and potentially for service delivery.
findings.figures: None quantified; forward-looking risk
findings.quote: The wider sustainability of current Scotland-wide levels of funding for adult social care services without significant service reductions is being increasingly questioned.

findings.paper_title: 7.3 Budget Strategy Update and MTFP
findings.headline: Teachers' pension contribution rates expected to fall from 28.68% to 17.68% from April 2027, potentially saving Edinburgh £2.2m per 1% reduction.
findings.detail: A UK Government increase in the SCAPE discount rate is driving a significant decrease in teachers' pension contribution rates across the UK. The English Teachers' Scheme is falling from 28.68% to 17.68%. However, the saving depends entirely on whether the Scottish Government passes through the resulting negative Consequentials from reduced departmental budgets—this decision has not yet been made. Additionally, the Scottish Pension Agency will not complete the Scottish Teachers' Scheme valuation until end of 2026, with final results expected in January/February 2027, after councils must set their budgets. This timing creates material uncertainty despite the scale of potential savings.
findings.matters: This could free up £20m+ per annum to help close the budget gap if passed through, but remains wholly contingent on Scottish Government decisions and the outcome of a valuation not yet complete. It represents both a major potential solution and a major source of uncertainty in the MTFP.
findings.figures: 28.68% to 17.68% rate reduction; each 1% change = £2.2m for Edinburgh
findings.quote: This is resulting in a significant decrease in employers' contributions (e.g. the Teachers' scheme reducing from 28.68% to 17.68%) from April 2027.

findings.paper_title: 7.3 Budget Strategy Update and MTFP
findings.headline: Edinburgh faces a £14.3m funding gap for 2027/28, assuming full delivery of prior-year savings and no increase in demand.
findings.detail: The gap is stated explicitly in section 4.16 and depends on two critical assumptions: that all approved 2026/27 budget savings are fully delivered, and that service demand (particularly in homelessness and adult social care) does not materially increase. Any slippage in savings or surge in demand would increase the gap. The council must close this gap through new savings or other means by November 2026 when the detailed budget proposals are presented.
findings.matters: This is Edinburgh's core budget challenge. Any failure to deliver prior-year savings or emerging demand pressures would materially worsen the position and create pressure on reserves or borrowing.
findings.quote: The MTFP update to the previous meeting of the Committee on 23 June 2026 pointed to an estimated funding gap for 2027/28 of £14.3m.

findings.paper_title: 8.1 Capital Outturn_2025-26
findings.headline: Estimated total loan charges on 2025-26 capital borrowing: £626.3m General Fund and £303.8m HRA over 50-year repayment periods at assumed 5.25% loans fund rate.
findings.detail: General Fund borrowing of £216.6m principal will generate £409.7m interest over 50 years. HRA borrowing of £105.1m principal will generate £198.7m interest. Combined long-tail loan charges total £930.1m. Both revenue budgets are committed to servicing these charges, and the cost is sensitive to changes in the assumed loans fund rate.
findings.matters: Capital expenditure creates decades of revenue commitment. The £930.1m aggregate loan charge is a structural revenue burden. Variations from the 5.25% rate assumption would materially alter effective costs.
findings.figures: General Fund: £216.6m principal, £409.7m interest = £626.3m total (£12.5m average annual over 50 years); HRA: £105.1m principal, £198.7m interest = £303.8m total (£6.1m average annual over 50 years); combined £930.1m in loan charges; assumed loans fund rate 5.25%
findings.quote: The estimated loans charges associated with 2025-26 General Fund outturn amount to a principal repayment of £216.6m and interest of £409.7m. This would be a total cost of £626.3m with an average annual repayment of £12.5m over 50 years, based on an assumed loans fund interest rate of 5.25%.

findings.paper_title: 8.1 Capital Outturn_2025-26
findings.headline: Housing acquisitions for homelessness: 1,004 homes approved since November 2023 housing emergency declaration, but only 598 completed and handed over (60% delivery rate).
findings.detail: Since declaring a housing emergency in November 2023, the council approved 1,004 home purchases to combat homelessness. Only 598 have been completed and handed over, a 60% completion rate. A further ~540 are under construction and ~5,500 in design or pre-construction, indicating multi-year delivery ahead. New housebuilding delivered 306 homes in 2025-26.
findings.matters: The housing emergency is a driver of capital spending and revenue pressure. A 60% completion rate on approved acquisitions and large pipeline in early design stages suggest full delivery will require sustained capital investment and revenue resources over several years.
findings.figures: 1,004 homes approved since November 2023; 598 completed and handed over (60% completion); ~540 under construction; ~5,500 in design or pre-construction; 306 new homes delivered in 2025-26; £37.4m grant transferred to RSLs
findings.quote: As at year-end, and since November 2023, the Council had approved purchases of 1,004 homes from private developers. Of these, 598 homes have been completed and handed over to the Council.

findings.paper_title: 8.1 Capital Outturn_2025-26
findings.headline: High-Rise housing programmes reprofiled with Fire Safety extended from 3-year to 4-year delivery (£13.8m) and Retrofit delayed at two sites due to redesign (£12.0m).
findings.detail: The Fire Safety Programme was reset to original 4-year timeline after attempted acceleration, indicating delivery risk. The High-Rise Retrofit Programme has experienced site start delays at Craigmillar/Peffermill and Cables Wynd/Linksview requiring design changes. Combined £25.8m of material HRA spending is experiencing schedule slippage.
findings.matters: High-Rise works are life-safety and energy-efficiency critical. Schedule delays extend the timeline for these priority works and defer their revenue benefits.
findings.figures: Fire Safety Programme £13.8m extended to 4-year plan; Retrofit Programme £12.0m with site delays at two locations; combined £25.8m of capital spending affected
findings.quote: A significant amount of this was expenditure related to the High-Rise estate with the Fire Safety Programme (£13.8m) being revised back to the original four-year plan instead of three to allow better control over delivery, and the High Rise Retrofit Programme (£12.0m) seeing site start delays at Craigmillar/Peffermill and Cables Wynd/Linksview as a result of redesign.

findings.paper_title: 8.1 Capital Outturn_2025-26
findings.headline: MacMillan Hub project incurred £1.6m overspend due to unforeseen building conditions, with cost-sharing with partner North Edinburgh Arts still unresolved.
findings.detail: The library element overspent by £1.6m from discovery of unforeseen site conditions. The final allocation of costs between the council and North Edinburgh Arts partner remains outstanding, meaning council liability could increase pending resolution.
findings.matters: Unquantified project overruns and unresolved cost-sharing arrangements create budget uncertainty and introduce disputes with third parties.
findings.figures: £1.6m overspend; final cost allocation between Council and North Edinburgh Arts outstanding
findings.quote: The MacMillan Hub project has incurred an overspend (£1.6m) due to unforeseen building conditions. The final allocation of costs between the North Edinburgh Arts and the Council's library element remains outstanding

findings.paper_title: 8.1 Capital Outturn_2025-26
findings.headline: Capital receipts from asset sales achieved £5.7m of £9.9m budgeted (57% shortfall), with the recurring £3m annual receipt not materialising and Granton Waterfront land sale pushed to future years.
findings.detail: Asset sales underperformed by £4.2m. The recurring £3m annual receipt from the corporate property programme did not occur in 2025-26, and a £1.2m land receipt from Granton Waterfront is now delayed. This creates both a one-year shortfall and raises questions about the reliability of assumed recurring receipts.
findings.matters: Capital receipts are relied on to fund capital projects. A 42% shortfall reduces non-borrowed funding and forces increased reliance on loans, raising long-term debt levels.
findings.figures: £5.7m receipts achieved vs £9.9m budget (£4.2m shortfall or 42%); recurring receipt assumption £3m did not materialise; Granton Waterfront land receipt £1.2m delayed
findings.quote: Asset sales of £5.7m were achieved against a budget of £9.9m. The capital budget assumes a recurring £3m of receipts each year as part of the ongoing corporate property programme, but they did not materialise in 2025-26.

findings.paper_title: 8.1 Capital Outturn_2025-26
findings.headline: Borrowing requirement reduced by £28.4m due to capital spending delays, deferring £1.6m of loans charges to 2026-27 and beyond.
findings.detail: Delayed capital expenditure (£38.2m) and funding shortfalls (£9.8m) combined to reduce Loans Fund Advances by £28.4m. This creates a cash timing benefit in 2025-26 but transfers revenue pressure to future years when deferred spending occurs. Delayed housing acquisitions will continue to be serviced via third-party providers at higher cost in the interim.
findings.matters: Capital spending delays defer revenue loan charges, but future-year revenue budgets must absorb these charges when spending is completed. The shift to expensive interim provision masks the true cost of the delay.
findings.figures: Loans Fund Advances requirement reduced by £28.4m; revenue loans charges of £1.6m deferred from 2026-27; expenditure delays £38.2m; funding shortfall £9.8m
findings.quote: Delays in expenditure noted above and the reduction in funding have therefore lowered the requirement for loans fund advances by £28.4m when compared to budget.

findings.paper_title: 8.1 Capital Outturn_2025-26
findings.headline: General Fund capital spending underspent by £38.2m (9%), with housing acquisitions for temporary accommodation delayed by £20m due to insufficient available properties.
findings.detail: The council acquired 147 of 222 planned temporary accommodation units, missing the target by 66 units. The shortage reflects real estate market constraints rather than demand reduction. The council also acknowledged over-optimistic initial forecasting by deliberately reducing the revised budget by £21m to allow for anticipated slippage, indicating systematic forecasting challenges.
findings.matters: A 9% underspend suggests execution risk or forecasting inaccuracy. Temporary accommodation acquisition delays perpetuate reliance on higher-cost third-party provision, creating hidden revenue pressure.
findings.figures: £388.3m outturn vs £426.4m revised budget (£38.2m or 9.0% underspend); housing acquisitions £20.0m shortfall; 147 of 222 units acquired; budget deliberately reduced by £21.0m for over-optimistic forecasts
findings.quote: Delays to expenditure in the Housing Acquisitions for Temporary Accommodation programme (£20.0m) whereby the availability of former council houses or suitable homes on the open market was much less than anticipated.

findings.paper_title: The City of Edinburgh Council – 2025-26 Annual Audit Report
findings.headline: The Council's approach to strategic asset management is fragmented, making it harder to make well-informed decisions about priorities.
findings.detail: In the Best Value section of the audit, the Management Report on themes prescribed by the Accounts Commission identified that the Council's strategic asset management approach is fragmented. This fragmentation affects the Council's ability to make well-informed decisions about resource and capital priorities.
findings.matters: Fragmented asset management impairs capital investment decision-making and can lead to inefficient resource deployment; affects long-term financial sustainability and value for money.
findings.figures: No figures provided.
findings.quote: The Council's approach to strategic asset management is fragmented, which makes it harder for the Council to make well-informed decisions about priorities.

findings.paper_title: The City of Edinburgh Council – 2025-26 Annual Audit Report
findings.headline: The Council achieved an overall underspend of £32.202m in 2025/26 with an unqualified audit opinion.
findings.detail: The external auditor concluded that the annual accounts are free from material misstatement and show a true and fair view, following relevant accounting standards and legislation. The Council reported an overall surplus of £32.202m, with no change to this position arising from the audit process.
findings.matters: A clean audit opinion and significant surplus demonstrate financial control, compliance, and strong liquidity position; material to lender confidence in management capacity.
findings.figures: £32.202m overall underspend; no change arising from audit.
findings.quote: Subject to completion of Audit Scotland's internal review processes and satisfactory receipt of an agreed set of accounts, the external auditor has concluded that the annual accounts are free from material misstatement and considered to show a true and fair view and follow relevant accounting standards and legislation. The report also concludes that the Council has effective and appropriate arrangements in place for securing sound financial management, with an overall surplus of £32.202m reported.

findings.paper_title: The City of Edinburgh Council – 2025-26 Annual Audit Report
findings.headline: The audit found governance weaknesses that need to be addressed for arrangements to be effective.
findings.detail: While the auditor concluded the Council has appropriate arrangements for Vision and Leadership, it identified that the Council needs to address a number of weaknesses in governance for those arrangements to be effective. Three specific audit action points for the Council are set out in the auditor's report.
findings.matters: Governance weaknesses affect the control environment and risk management; they are material to both auditor confidence and lender assessment of management capacity.
findings.figures: Three action points identified.
findings.quote: The report concludes that the Council has appropriate arrangements in place for Vision and Leadership but needs to address a number of weaknesses in governance for arrangements to be effective.

findings.paper_title: The City of Edinburgh Council – 2025-26 Annual Audit Report
findings.headline: An objection to housing and homelessness disclosures led the auditor to require additional information to be added to the audited accounts.
findings.detail: During the 15-day public inspection period, an individual objected to the Council's financial statements on grounds of statutory duties relating to housing and homelessness. The objection raised matters relating to disclosures in the Annual Governance Statement, Management Commentary, and financial statements. Audit Scotland sought additional evidence from management and, having considered the matter, requested additional disclosures be made to the annual accounts, which were subsequently amended.
findings.matters: The auditor's requirement for additional disclosures indicates material gaps in initial disclosure of a statutory duty area; this suggests substantive issues with housing and homelessness provisions that were not initially fully transparent.
findings.figures: One objection received; disclosures amended to address it.
findings.quote: One objection was received in respect of the Council's financial statements. The objection received centred on the Council's statutory duties in relation to housing and homelessness. Specifically, it raised a number of matters relating to disclosures within the Annual Governance Statement, Management Commentary and the financial statements. Audit Scotland sought additional evidence and assurances from management and having considered the matter, requested additional disclosures to be made to the annual accounts which were amended as a result.

findings.paper_title: The City of Edinburgh Council – 2025-26 Annual Audit Report
findings.headline: The Council plans to increase substantially borrowing and debt levels over the next five years, which presents a significant risk to its longer-term financial sustainability.
findings.detail: The wider scope audit identified that the Council has broadly effective financial management and sustainability arrangements. findings.detail: General Fund reserves grew £48.162m to £349.479m. findings.paper_title: 8.3 Revenue monitoring outturn 25-26
findings.headline: Council Tax income fell £1.7m due to reduction in tax base buoyancy—a structural revenue loss.
findings.detail: Council Tax revenue shortfall of £1.7m is attributed to "a reduction in tax base buoyancy relative to recent years". Tax base buoyancy is new revenue from property growth and revaluation; a sustained reduction indicates either no growth in the property tax base or downward revaluations, signalling loss of economic activity or property values in the area and a permanent reduction in available revenue.
findings.matters: Council Tax is the most stable revenue source; a structural loss in buoyancy indicates the council's permanent revenue base has contracted and forward budgets cannot assume return to prior growth rates.

findings.matters: A 30% shortfall rate in approved savings is a leading indicator of weak budget control in the council's largest, most volatile service areas; it will likely recur in 2026/27 and beyond unless underlying practices change.

findings.paper_title: Item 7.2 - Treasury Management - Annual Report 2025-26
findings.headline: Council deliberately borrowed short-dated loans to reduce costs, accepting medium-term refinancing risk
findings.detail: The council chose to borrow at the shorter end of the yield curve to achieve rates below budget, while explicitly accepting 'additional medium-term re-financing risk.' This strategy makes sense if short rates remain benign but exposes the council if short-term rates spike when these loans mature.
findings.matters: This is a directional bet on the shape of the yield curve; it trades near-term savings for extended vulnerability to short-rate shocks and shows the council is already managing to budget constraints.

findings.matters: Annual debt costs are now material to the council's revenue budget; a trend of rapid increases forecasts pressure on general fund finances if rates remain elevated or new borrowing is required.

Two senior leadership changes in critical finance and operations roles within six months raises questions about operational continuity.

findings.figures: CFO changed 15 May 2026; COO changed October 2025
findings.quote: On 15 May 2026, Jennifer O'Brien replaced Alan Sievewright as Chief Financial Officer following his resignation.

findings.paper_title: Item 7.1 - Appendix 1 - 2026 - Unaudited Financial Statements
findings.headline: Cyber security listed as one of the seven highest enterprise risks with potential for service disruption
findings.detail: Cyber threats are explicitly identified as one of the council's seven highest current-risk enterprise issues. The risk statement warns that if adequate cyber arrangements are not in place—both technically and culturally—an attack could occur that the council is unprepared to respond to. This could result in legal, service delivery, financial and reputational impacts. While mitigating actions are listed, the risk remains elevated.
findings.matters: A cyber incident that disrupts council finance systems, payroll, or revenue collection could trigger a liquidity crisis or prevent the council from collecting council tax and business rates. This is a material operational risk that a lender should monitor.
findings.figures: Cyber risk ranked in top 7 enterprise risks as of March 2026
findings.quote: If adequate cyber arrangements are not in place, both technically (from a resilience/preparedness perspective) as well as culturally (employees understanding their roles and responsibilities in terms of prevention), an attack could occur that the Council is unprepared to respond to adequately, adversely impacting the delivery of essential services. This risk could have legal, service delivery, financial and/or reputational impacts for the Council.

findings.paper_title: Item 7.1 - Appendix 1 - 2026 - Unaudited Financial Statements
findings.headline: Finance service initiated transformation programme to address internal control challenges
findings.detail: In 2025, the council initiated a comprehensive Finance Divisional Transformation Programme, explicitly recognising "a need for change within the Finance service to respond to a range of internal and external challenges." The Finance Assurance Board, established to provide senior grip on financial performance, has experienced variable directorate attendance. A review of its format and membership is now underway. Budget accountability letters are being issued to all directors.
findings.matters: This signals that current financial controls and budget accountability were not operating as needed. A lender assesses credit risk partly on whether the council's finance function can reliably forecast and manage expenditure. Recent control improvements are positive, but the fact that they were needed is a red flag.
findings.figures: Phase 1 of Divisional Transformation initiated 2025
findings.quote: recognising a need for change within the Finance service to respond to a range of internal and external challenges, in 2025 a comprehensive Divisional Transformation Programme was initiated, with key initial priorities being development and associated delivery of robust savings plans, moves towards adopting a more zero-based budgeting approach to resource allocation and wider workstreams around delivering improvements in systems, business intelligence and data strategy.

findings.paper_title: Item 7.1 - Appendix 1 - 2026 - Unaudited Financial Statements
findings.headline: £1.6 billion housing investment commitment creates long-term capital debt obligations
findings.detail: The council has committed to a transformational £1.6bn five-year housing investment programme in response to the housing emergency. This is one of the largest housing interventions by a local authority in modern times. The programme is designed to eliminate use of unsuitable accommodation, but it creates a decade-long debt servicing obligation that will constrain financial flexibility during the period when £93m in other savings are also due.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand how this capital programme will be financed (borrowing, grants, reserves) and how debt servicing costs will interact with the concurrent revenue savings cliff. If both pressures hit simultaneously and the housing programme underperforms, the council could face a refinancing crisis.
findings.figures: £1.6 billion over five years
findings.quote: a comprehensive review of Homelessness expenditure was undertaken to develop a transformative £1.6bn 5-year housing investment programme which aims to optimise positive outcomes and eliminate use of unsuitable accommodation and exceptionally high-cost temporary accommodation.

findings.paper_title: Item 7.1 - Appendix 1 - 2026 - Unaudited Financial Statements
findings.headline: 6,521 households in temporary accommodation as of March 2026 with 51.5% failure-to-accommodate rate flagged as regulatory risk
findings.detail: The council faces acute housing pressures with over 6,521 households in temporary accommodation as of March 2026. The failure rate (households unable to be accommodated) is running at 51.5%. This is explicitly flagged as a regulatory risk with legal, financial and reputational impacts. The council is responding with a £1.6bn five-year investment programme, but immediate spending on temporary accommodation continues to spike.
findings.matters: This is a direct driver of growing uncontrollable expenditure. Temporary accommodation costs are typically 2-3x higher than permanent housing. A lender assessing sustainability must know whether the £1.6bn programme can actually reduce this demand, or whether spending will continue escalating.
findings.figures: 6,521 households in temporary accommodation; 51.5% failure-to-accommodate rate
findings.quote: The Council is facing acute housing-related pressures due to high housing costs and homelessness rates, with over 6,521 households in temporary accommodation as of March 2026. If demand continues to outstrip supply, it may be unable to provide accommodation or deliver the service required, with the failure to accommodate rate of households presenting as homeless remaining high at around 51.5%.

findings.paper_title: Item 7.1 - Appendix 1 - 2026 - Unaudited Financial Statements
findings.headline: £93m savings requirement over four years with no fallback if delivery slips
findings.detail: Current financial projections show the council needs £14.3m recurring savings in 2027/28, rising to £93m cumulatively by 2030/31. The position assumes full delivery of all approved savings and robust management of residual service pressures. If either assumption breaks, there is no identified funding solution. This cliff emerges immediately after the 2026/27 balanced budget.
findings.matters: A lender needs confidence the council can credibly deliver this scale of savings. If the plan fails, Edinburgh faces a structural deficit it cannot close through income alone.
findings.quote: Current projections indicate a need to deliver at least £14.3m of recurring savings in 2027/28, increasing to £93m over the four-year period to 2030/31 as shown in the chart below: The position presented assumes robust management of all residual service pressures and full delivery of all approved savings.

findings.paper_title: Item 7.7 - Budget Strategy and Medium-Term Financial Plan (MTFP) 202631 – progress update
findings.headline: Council's finances remain highly sensitive to government grant funding and inflation assumptions
findings.detail: The council identifies its MTFP as sensitive to 'relatively small changes' in core government funding and inflation. This means planning assumptions are fragile and actual outturn could diverge materially if national funding or inflation trends move from forecast.
findings.matters: Planning dependencies on volatile external variables (government grants, inflation) that are outside the council's control create additional downside risk and limit the predictability of future deficits and borrowing needs.
findings.figures: Sensitivity to government grant core funding and inflation highlighted
findings.quote: The Council's finances remain very sensitive to relatively small changes in key planning assumptions e.g. government grant core funding, inflation.

findings.paper_title: Item 7.7 - Budget Strategy and Medium-Term Financial Plan (MTFP) 202631 – progress update
findings.headline: £32.6m savings programme is still in early delivery stage with acknowledged risks requiring mitigation
findings.detail: The 2026/27 budget includes £32.6m of approved savings. However, the report notes explicitly that this is 'at an early point in time' and that officers will need to 'address any challenges and consider mitigations as required'. No indication of delivery confidence is provided.
findings.matters: A large, nascent savings programme carries execution risk. If savings do not materialise on schedule, the £14.3m gap for 2027/28 could widen further, forcing either deeper mid-year cuts or reserve use.
findings.figures: £32.6m savings programme for 2026/27
findings.quote: It should be noted that these dashboards are as at an early point in time in the financial year. Officers will continue to progress delivery of all approved savings and investments proposals and address any challenges and consider mitigations as required.

findings.paper_title: Item 7.7 - Budget Strategy and Medium-Term Financial Plan (MTFP) 202631 – progress update
findings.headline: Downside scenario shows budget gap could reach £42.4m in 2027/28, nearly three times the baseline forecast
findings.detail: Sensitivity analysis modelling identifies a potential worst-case scenario for 2027/28 with a £42.4m deficit. The council describes itself as 'very sensitive' to changes in assumptions around government grants and inflation, indicating significant planning uncertainty.
findings.matters: Lenders need to understand downside risk to borrowing requirements and reserve depletion. A gap nearly 3× the baseline would require either severe service cuts, large council tax increases, or substantial reserve drawdown, any of which would materially affect creditworthiness.
findings.figures: £42.4m potential 2027/28 gap in downside scenario vs £14.3m baseline
findings.quote: The 'downside' scenario reflects a potential 2027/28 budget gap of up to £42.4m.

findings.paper_title: Item 7.7 - Budget Strategy and Medium-Term Financial Plan (MTFP) 202631 – progress update
findings.headline: Projected budget gap for 2027/28 has increased by 68% from February forecast
findings.detail: In February 2026, the council projected a £8.5m shortfall for 2027/28; this June update raises it to £14.3m. The cumulative gap by 2030/31 has risen from £63.2m to £93.0m. This represents a material deterioration in the medium-term financial position within four months.
findings.matters: Lenders assess council borrowing risk partly on medium-term deficit trajectory. A 48% increase in cumulative deficit over a 5-year horizon signals either weaker underlying finances than previously forecast or greater pressure on reserves and borrowing capacity.
findings.figures: £14.3m gap 2027/28 (up from £8.5m); £93.0m cumulative by 2030/31 (up from £63.2m)
findings.quote: The Council's updated Medium-Term Financial Plan (MTFP) projections reflect an estimated budget gap of £14.3m for 2027/28 and a cumulative budget gap of £93.0m by 2030/31.

findings.paper_title: Item 7.5 - Capital Strategy 2026-36 – Annual Report – referral from Finance and Resources Committee - Appendix
findings.headline: Council has already cut £400m from running costs over the last decade, reducing flexibility to find further savings.
findings.detail: Section 5.4 notes: "in the last decade the Council has saved over £400 million from its annual running costs." This is substantial cost reduction already undertaken. It suggests the council has limited remaining flexibility to deliver the savings required to close the £66m gap, and leaves little room for error if pressures (pay awards, demographic demand, cost-of-living impacts) exceed assumptions.
findings.matters: A lender assessing the credibility of the budget should note that the council has already made deep cuts. The likelihood of finding another £66m in permanent recurring savings becomes lower when £400m has already been removed from a budget that cycles around £1.3bn in revenue.
findings.figures: £400m saved from annual running costs over the last decade; annual revenue spend is over £1.3bn
findings.quote: in the last decade the Council has saved over £400 million from its annual running costs

findings.paper_title: Item 7.5 - Capital Strategy 2026-36 – Annual Report – referral from Finance and Resources Committee - Appendix
findings.headline: Council debt is projected to more than double over five years, from £2.5bn to £5.1bn, with Capital Financing Requirement reaching £5.5bn.
findings.detail: The ambitious capital programme, including the Housing Emergency intervention, results in progressive year-on-year increases in borrowing. Chart 2 shows the CFR growing from £2,850m (2025/26) to £5,478m (2029/30). This is driven by £4.06bn in Loans Fund Advances over the 10-year period.
