The strategy acknowledges this as a significant constraint: "The Council's capital resources are limited. Borrowing carried out for investment must be repaid from increasingly limited revenue budgets."
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand leverage and headroom. Doubling debt in 5 years is material, especially when paired with HRA debt servicing hitting 67% and a £66m revenue gap emerging. The strategy assumes 5.25% interest rates; borrowing already done at 4.60% (2025/26) shows rates could be lower, but also that they could be higher.
findings.figures: Debt grows from £2,528m (2025/26 forecast) to £5,161m (2029/30); CFR to £5,478m (2029/30); £4,063m of Loans Fund Advances over the 10-year period
findings.quote: The ambitious capital programme, including the significant intervention to address the Housing Emergency, has resulted in progressive year on year increases in the Capital Financing Requirement, more than doubling the Council's debt over five years.

findings.paper_title: Item 7.5 - Capital Strategy 2026-36 – Annual Report – referral from Finance and Resources Committee - Appendix
findings.headline: General Fund faces a £66m budget gap by 2029-30 with no funding solution yet identified.
findings.detail: The strategy is balanced for 2026/27 but significant challenges emerge in future years. Section 5.10 explicitly states that the annual funding gap is expected to increase to £66m for the Council (and a further £60m for the Edinburgh Integrated Joint Board) by 2029-30. This gap threatens both revenue stability and the capital programme's deliverability.
findings.matters: A lender needs confidence that the council can balance its revenue budget to comply with the Prudential Code. An unresolved gap of this magnitude 3-4 years out is material. The strategy itself notes that failure to close it may require reductions to capital expenditure plans (section 7.7).
findings.figures: £66m annual gap for Council, £60m for Integrated Joint Board, expected by 2029-30
findings.quote: there are significant challenges in future years with the annual gap expected to increase to £66m for the Council and a further £60m for the Edinburgh Integrated Joint Board by 2029-30

findings.paper_title: Item 7.5 - Capital Strategy 2026-36 – Annual Report – referral from Finance and Resources Committee - Appendix
findings.headline: HRA debt servicing costs rising to 67% of rental income by 2030-31, leaving minimal headroom for maintenance or operations.
findings.detail: The Housing Revenue Account is financing major capital investment through borrowing, with debt servicing costs rising sharply from 38.6% in 2025/26 to 67.1% by 2030/31. This is driven by the Housing Emergency investment programme. The strategy notes this is "affordable and prudent" but the trajectory is steep, and section 5.11 warns that if rents don't increase as assumed, capital investment will need to be scaled back.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know the HRA can service its debt and maintain housing stock. At 67%, there is very little buffer for rent shortfalls, maintenance backlogs, or interest rate rises beyond the assumed 5.25%.
findings.figures: HRA debt servicing 38.6% (2025/26) → 67.1% (2030/31); General Fund debt servicing 8.3% (2025/26) → 11.1% (2030/31)
findings.quote: Proportion of net HRA revenue stream ... 67.10%

findings.paper_title: 7.3 CEC Treasury Management Strategy 26-27 with appendices_FINAL
findings.headline: Council seeking new funding sources via Community Municipal Investments to supplement traditional PWLB borrowing.
findings.detail: The Treasury Strategy approves an initial Community Municipal Investment (CMI) launch in September 2026 with a £1m target. The paper describes CMIs as 'replacement borrowing' for approved capital projects, not new projects. However, the Council is actively opening a supplementary funding route, suggesting awareness that traditional borrowing capacity or appetite may be constrained.
findings.matters: CMIs are retail debt instruments; the fact the Council is pursuing them signals it is exploring all funding options. While CMIs may offer competitive rates, they represent additional public debt and add to the volume of Council borrowing in market.
findings.figures: CMI launch target £1 million; funds raised will be 'replacement borrowing' for pre-approved projects
findings.quote: CMIs are effectively replacement borrowing for projects already approved within the Council's capital budget... an initial issuance in September 2026... with a proposed fundraising target of £1 million.

findings.paper_title: 7.3 CEC Treasury Management Strategy 26-27 with appendices_FINAL
findings.headline: Loan repayment terms extended to 50 years for buildings and long-life assets to manage annual debt servicing costs.
findings.detail: On 5 February 2026, the Council approved changes extending the repayment term for buildings and long-life assets from their previous schedule to 50 years using the asset-life method on an annuity basis. This reduces annual repayment obligations but pushes debt repayment into the distant future, materially increasing the total interest cost of the debt.
findings.matters: Extended repayment periods reduce immediate cash flow pressure but increase total debt burden for future generations and reduce the Council's flexibility if circumstances change. A 50-year asset life assumes stable operations and income over half a century—a risky assumption for local government.
findings.figures: Repayment terms extended to 50 years for buildings and long-life assets; other assets 20–45 years
findings.quote: On 5 February 2026, the Council approved changes to the Loans Fund Advances repayment policy based on a prudent financial management strategy. This extended the repayment term of advances for buildings and long-life assets to 50 years.

findings.paper_title: 7.3 CEC Treasury Management Strategy 26-27 with appendices_FINAL
findings.headline: £30m LOBO loans called, requiring immediate refinancing during period of elevated interest rates.
findings.detail: The debt management section notes that £30m of LOBO (Lender's Option Borrower's Option) loans have been called. LOBO loans allow the lender to reset rates or force redemption; when called during a rising rate environment, the borrower must refinance at current (higher) market rates. This adds to the Council's refinancing risk during 2026/27.
findings.matters: Called LOBO loans force refinancing risk at a time of elevated rates. The Council cannot defer or negotiate; it must refinance these £30m at whatever rates are available, increasing near-term debt costs.
findings.figures: £30m of Council LOBO loans called
findings.quote: In addition, £30m of Council LOBO loans have been called which further increases the borrowing requirement.

findings.paper_title: 7.3 CEC Treasury Management Strategy 26-27 with appendices_FINAL
findings.headline: Asset sales declining across General Fund and HRA, reducing non-debt funding sources.
findings.detail: General Fund capital receipts from asset sales fall from £7.710m (2025/26) to £3.000m–£3.049m by 2029–2031. HRA asset sales fall from £31.888m (2025/26) to £21.965m (2030/31). This shrinking revenue source forces greater reliance on borrowing to fund the capital programme, removing flexibility to reduce debt take-on.
findings.matters: Declining asset sales mean the Council has fewer options to fund capital without borrowing. If asset sales fall faster than forecast—a common occurrence during economic slowdown—the Council must either cut capital, increase borrowing, or raid reserves.
findings.quote: Table A2.1 shows Funding Sources for General Fund Services Capital Expenditure... Asset Sales: 7.710 [2025/26]... 3.000... 3.049 [2029/31]

findings.paper_title: 7.3 CEC Treasury Management Strategy 26-27 with appendices_FINAL
findings.headline: Council borrowing £1.01bn in single year (2028/29) while Treasury advises long-term interest rates will not fall.
findings.detail: Table A2.3 shows planned PWLB borrowing peaking at £1.01bn in 2028/29. Simultaneously, the Council's Treasury Advisors' forecast (Appendix 1, Figure A1.4) shows 20-year Gilt yields not expected to fall from current elevated levels. The paper explicitly states the situation is 'worrisome', and the Council borrowed £350m in 2025/26 at an average rate of 4.60%—substantially above the long-term assumption of 5.25% used in debt servicing calculations.
findings.matters: The Council is committing to borrow over £1bn in a single year at rates that may not decline, locking in high interest costs for decades. The gap between assumed servicing rate (5.25%) and actual borrowing rate (4.60%) is narrow; any rate rise above 5.25% immediately strains debt servicing capacity.
findings.figures: Planned PWLB borrowing 2028/29: £1,010,000k; borrowing in 2025/26 at 4.60% average; 20-year Gilt yields expected broadly stable; assumed interest rate 5.25%
findings.quote: At a time when long term interest rates remain relatively high, the Council has a substantial borrowing requirement over the next few years... The fact that Gilt Yields are not expected to fall when the Council has a substantial borrowing requirement is worrisome.

findings.paper_title: 7.3 CEC Treasury Management Strategy 26-27 with appendices_FINAL
findings.headline: HRA debt service costs rising to 67.1% of revenue stream by 2030/31, from 38.6% currently, creating sustainability risk.
findings.detail: The Prudential Indicators show HRA financing costs as a proportion of revenue rising from 38.6% in 2025/26 to 67.1% by 2030/31. The most acute stress occurs in 2029/30–2030/31, precisely when the housing emergency capital programme is at its peak, with planned HRA borrowing of £498.9m and £237.5m respectively. This trajectory shows housing-funded debt servicing consuming two-thirds of rental revenue.
findings.matters: HRA cannot be subsidised from general fund; if debt service consumes 67% of revenue, the HRA has minimal flexibility for maintenance, improvements, or tenant support. This creates operational risk and signals the housing programme is unsustainable at these debt levels without major income growth or spending cuts.
findings.quote: Housing Revenue Account (HRA) 38.6% 38.6% 40.2% 51.3% 62.2% 67.1%

findings.paper_title: 7.3 CEC Treasury Management Strategy 26-27 with appendices_FINAL
findings.headline: Council's cumulative borrowing need rising to £5.332bn by 31 March 2031, more than doubling the current capital financing requirement.
findings.detail: The Council is forecasting total capital expenditure of £4.770bn between 2025/26 and 2030/31, with underlying borrowing need increasing to £5.332bn. Figure 1.2 shows cumulative capital funded by borrowing more than doubling over the next five years. This substantial and escalating debt burden reflects the Council's commitment to capital investment, particularly in response to the housing emergency.
findings.matters: Lenders need to understand the quantum and trajectory of debt the Council will carry. A £5.3bn cumulative need represents a major expansion of the Council's debt position and creates refinancing risk across the forecast period.
findings.figures: £4.770bn total capital expenditure 2025/26–2030/31; underlying need to borrow £5.332bn at 31 March 2031
findings.quote: The Council's total capital expenditure is forecast to be £4.770bn between 2025/26 and 2030/31... the Council's underlying need to borrow (shown as 'Cumulative Capital Expenditure') is projected to increase to £5.332bn at 31 March 2031.

findings.paper_title: Item 4.2(c) - Approaches to HRA Debt Financing - Appendix 1
findings.headline: Council rejected four explicit options to remain within 50% debt target in favour of prioritising housing investment
findings.detail: The paper presents four clear pathways to keep debt financing below 50%: reduce existing home investment by £287m (22%), reduce new homes investment by £344m (affecting 988 homes), increase rents 14% above current plans, or contribute £113m from general fund. The council chose none of these, preferring the Housing Emergency response over debt targets.
findings.matters: This demonstrates that policy priorities (housing supply in response to an emergency) can override stated financial prudence benchmarks, which affects stability of future borrowing decisions and risk appetite.
findings.figures: Option A: £287m reduction (22%); Option B: £344m reduction (42%, 988 homes); Option C: 14% rent increase; Option D: £113m subsidy
findings.quote: Should members wish to ensure this ratio remains below 50%, the following options are available: On 15 January 2026, Finance and Resources Committee considered a report on the Loans Fund Policy Review

findings.paper_title: Item 4.2(c) - Approaches to HRA Debt Financing - Appendix 1
findings.headline: Council debt has more than doubled over five years and will continue to grow substantially under officer proposals
findings.detail: The council states that the capital investment programme, together with general fund investment in temporary housing, has resulted in the Capital Financing Requirement more than doubling over five years. Debt servicing costs are projected to rise from £49m in 2025/26 to £148m by 2035/36 (a 200% increase), while HRA income only rises from £128m to £265m.
findings.matters: Rapidly rising debt-to-income ratios combined with sustained capital expansion reduces financial flexibility and limits refinancing options if market conditions change.
findings.figures: Debt doubled over 5 years; debt servicing £49m (2025/26) → £148m (2035/36); income £128m (2025/26) → £265m (2035/36)
findings.quote: This ambitious capital programme, together with significant general fund investment in temporary housing, has resulted in progressive year on year increases in the Capital Financing Requirement, more than doubling the Council's debt over five years.

findings.paper_title: Item 4.2(c) - Approaches to HRA Debt Financing - Appendix 1
findings.headline: Audit Scotland flagged risks in the HRA's current financing approach and specifically called for this report on alternatives
findings.detail: The council notes that Audit Scotland highlighted risks associated with the financing approach and called for a report detailing alternative methods to keep debt below 50%. This report was explicitly commissioned in response to external audit concern about sustainability. The audit recommendation appears in the council's own September 2025 decision record.
findings.matters: An independent auditor's concern about HRA debt sustainability is a governance flag. The council's decision to proceed with higher leverage despite the audit warning is material to lender risk assessment.
findings.figures: Report requested in 'two cycles' to address audit concerns
findings.quote: Council notes Audit Scotland has highlighted the risks associated with this financing approach and calls for a report in two cycles to Housing, Homelessness and Fair Work Committee detailing alternative approaches that keep debt financing below 50% of spend and further methods to mitigate the risks involved

findings.paper_title: Item 4.2(c) - Approaches to HRA Debt Financing - Appendix 1
findings.headline: Council projects HRA debt financing ratio to reach 67.1% by 2030/31, significantly exceeding the 50% benchmark it was asked to defend
findings.detail: The council's officer budget proposals include £780m of additional housing investment that will drive the debt financing ratio from 39.5% in 2024/25 to 67.1% by 2030/31. This exceeds the 50% target that was the stated target of the report requested by full council. The paper acknowledges the trajectory will be concerning (60% by 2029/30) but concludes the position remains 'affordable, prudent and sustainable.'
findings.matters: A council explicitly choosing higher leverage than stated benchmarks, justified by policy priority rather than financial metrics, signals both higher debt service risk and potential volatility in future borrowing decisions.
findings.figures: 39.5% (2024/25), 67.1% by 2030/31, £780m additional investment
findings.quote: The ratio of HRA financing costs to income is also projected to increase to 67.1% by 2030/31. However, this position has been reviewed alongside the Council's reserves position and wider financial strategy and is considered to be affordable and prudent.

findings.paper_title: Item 4.2(b) - Housing Revenue Account Budget Strategy 2026-27 – 2035-36 Risks and Reserves - referral from the Finance and Resources Committee - Appendix
findings.headline: General Fund subsidy of £38.598m required to hold HRA reserves at minimum £25m
findings.detail: The forecast that general reserves remain at or above £25m for all ten years depends on a proposed General Fund contribution of £38.598m. This means the HRA cannot sustain its planned capital programme and minimum reserves on rental income and borrowing alone; it requires recurring subsidy from the council's general finances.
findings.matters: A lender to the HRA or council would need to know that HRA sustainability relies on ongoing subsidy from general fund finances, which are themselves under pressure across English and Scottish local government.
findings.figures: General Fund contribution: £38.598m
findings.quote: The forecast General Reserve balance is above or at £25m for all ten years of the business plan. This position is supported by a proposed General Fund contribution of £38.598m.

findings.paper_title: Item 4.2(b) - Housing Revenue Account Budget Strategy 2026-27 – 2035-36 Risks and Reserves - referral from the Finance and Resources Committee - Appendix
findings.headline: Future government grant funding is uncertain and planned to cease: assumes no AHSP grant increase after 2026/27
findings.detail: The plan assumes £15m/year Affordable Housing Supply Programme grant (£150m over ten years). Edinburgh's allocation for 2026/27 has not yet been advised. Additional Scottish Government acquisition funding that provided £28.685m in 2025/26 is assumed to stop entirely after 2025/26. The planning assumption states explicitly 'no further funding will be made available'.
findings.matters: If grant funding falls, the capital programme becomes unaffordable and must be cut or the HRA must borrow more, adding to debt service costs.
findings.figures: £15m/year AHSP assumed; £28.685m in 2025/26 acquisition funding assumed to end
findings.quote: The Scottish Government has provided National Acquisitions funding of an additional £14.882m in 2024/25 and £28.685m in 2025/26 for Edinburgh. This additional funding is ring fenced and can only be used to support the acquisition of new homes, and during 2024/25 for bringing void properties back into use, and cannot be used for ongoing development work. The planning assumption for the 2026/27 budget process is that no further funding will be made available.

findings.paper_title: Item 4.2(b) - Housing Revenue Account Budget Strategy 2026-27 – 2035-36 Risks and Reserves - referral from the Finance and Resources Committee - Appendix
findings.headline: Mid-market home transfer to Edinburgh Living at significant risk; current interest rates make transfer financially unviable for Edinburgh Living
findings.detail: The capital programme assumes all mid-market homes (579 of them) will transfer to Edinburgh Living at no cost to the HRA. At current interest rates, Edinburgh Living cannot afford this. The council is 'developing options' but has not resolved the problem; update expected in 2026/27.
findings.matters: If Edinburgh Living cannot take these homes, the HRA retains them and their ongoing operating costs and debt, consuming reserves or forcing cuts elsewhere.
findings.figures: 579 mid-market homes planned for transfer
findings.quote: Within the capital programme, there is an assumption that all mid-market homes will transfer to Edinburgh Living with all associated costs covered by the transfer. Based on current interest rates, there is a significant risk that this transfer will not be financially viable for Edinburgh Living.

findings.paper_title: Item 4.2(b) - Housing Revenue Account Budget Strategy 2026-27 – 2035-36 Risks and Reserves - referral from the Finance and Resources Committee - Appendix
findings.headline: Capital programme cost inflation: £2.879bn plan faces 'significant cost increases' on recent projects
findings.detail: The HRA has experienced significant cost inflation on capital projects in recent years and continues to see inflationary impacts on projects in development. The plan may require reprioritisation, cash-limiting budgets, and delaying uncommitted projects pending 'fully funded business cases'. No specific contingency buffer is disclosed.
findings.matters: Cost overruns on a £2.879bn programme would force either borrowing above assumption (adding to interest risk) or programme cuts, directly affecting the council's housing delivery targets.
findings.figures: Total capital programme: £2.879bn over 10 years
findings.quote: In view of significant cost increases on capital projects in recent years, and the ongoing inflationary impacts being seen on current projects being developed, there are risks that the cost of proposed projects will exceed the inflationary provision built into the capital programme.

findings.paper_title: Item 4.2(b) - Housing Revenue Account Budget Strategy 2026-27 – 2035-36 Risks and Reserves - referral from the Finance and Resources Committee - Appendix
findings.headline: Loans charges projected to rise from 38.6% to 65.8% of rental income by year 10, highly sensitive to interest rate changes
findings.detail: The business plan assumes borrowing at 5.25%. A 0.25% swing either way changes year 10 reserves by £35.75m. The jump from 38.6% to 65.8% of income committed to debt service is substantial; if interest rates remain higher than assumed, capital spending will need to be cut or reserves will be drawn faster.
findings.matters: At 65.8% of income, debt service becomes the HRA's largest cost. Rising interest rates could make the £2.879bn capital programme unaffordable, forcing programme delays or General Fund bailouts.
findings.figures: Loans charges: current 38.6% of income → 65.8% by year 10; 0.25% rate change = £35.75m reserve impact
findings.quote: There is a risk that the HRA will require to support additional borrowing and/or revenue running costs associated with projects contained within the existing programme. The 2026/27 business plan has been developed on the assumption that future borrowing is at 5.25%. However, for example, should future borrowing by 0.25% higher or lower than 5.25%, the impact on the forecast year ten reserves would be £35.75m, respectively.

findings.paper_title: Item 4.2(b) - Housing Revenue Account Budget Strategy 2026-27 – 2035-36 Risks and Reserves - referral from the Finance and Resources Committee - Appendix
findings.headline: Repairs and maintenance costs have significantly exceeded budget for three consecutive years
findings.detail: Actual repairs spending has overrun forecast spending in 2023/24, 2024/25, and 2025/26. The council is now investing additional money (£1.746m for high-rise planned maintenance, £0.48m for tenant safety including EICR and asbestos testing) but acknowledges the issue will be kept 'under ongoing review' without stating a solution.
findings.matters: A three-year pattern of overspend suggests either forecasting failure or structural cost issues. If this continues, it will erode reserves faster than projected.
findings.figures: Additional funding: £1.746m high-rise maintenance, £0.48m tenant safety
findings.quote: Repairs and maintenance has been an area where costs have significantly exceeded the level of budget provided in 2023/24, 2024/25 and 2025/26, therefore, this will be kept under ongoing review

findings.paper_title: Item 4.2(b) - Housing Revenue Account Budget Strategy 2026-27 – 2035-36 Risks and Reserves - referral from the Finance and Resources Committee - Appendix
findings.headline: A 1% reduction in planned rent increases would push the HRA into an £86m deficit by year 10
findings.detail: The business plan assumes 7% annual rent increases for years 1-8 and 3% for years 9-10. If increases fell to 6%, the plan loses £111m over the decade. Since year 10 reserves are forecast at only £25m, a 1% shortfall creates an £86m deficit. The plan has no buffer for lower rent growth.
findings.matters: Rent income is the HRA's primary revenue source. The sensitivity is extreme: a single percentage point miss on inflation or tenant acceptance of rises destroys decade-long financial stability.
findings.figures: 1% reduction = £86m deficit by year 10; 7% planned increases years 1-8, 3% years 9-10
findings.quote: should rent increases be reduced to 6% a year for years one to eight, this would result in c. £111m less income being generated over the ten years of the plan. The year ten reserves balance is currently estimated to be £25.0m, therefore the impact of a 1% reduction each year would place the HRA into a deficit position of £86m by year ten.

findings.paper_title: Item 4.1(d) - Capital Budget 2026-2036 - referral from the Finance and Resources Committee - Appendix
findings.headline: 42% of current capital programme is ringfenced with conditions; flexibility limited
findings.detail: Of the £1.7bn current programme, £691.8m (42%) is ringfenced funding with conditions (grants, capital receipts, developer contributions) or relates to prudentially funded projects. This limits the council's ability to reallocate budgets if priorities shift.
findings.matters: Limited discretion over existing budgets means any new pressures must be accommodated through additional borrowing or cuts to uncommitted projects.
findings.figures: Ringfenced funding £691.8m out of £1,663.8m (42%); committed funding £430.2m (26%); uncommitted £524.8m (32%)
findings.quote: £691.8m (42%) has ringfenced funding with conditions attached to grants, capital receipts or developer's contributions, or relates to prudentially funded projects.

findings.paper_title: Item 4.1(d) - Capital Budget 2026-2036 - referral from the Finance and Resources Committee - Appendix
findings.headline: General Fund financing costs increasing from 6.9% to 11% of revenue stream by 2030/31
findings.detail: The general services debt servicing ratio is projected to rise from 6.9% of net revenue in 2026/27 to 11% by 2030/31. This is a material increase in the fixed cost of the council's revenue budget, leaving less room for service spending or response to pressures.
findings.matters: As financing costs grow as a proportion of revenue, the council's flexibility to respond to demographic pressures (adult social care, children's services) or invest in service improvements is reduced.

findings.paper_title: Item 4.1(d) - Capital Budget 2026-2036 - referral from the Finance and Resources Committee - Appendix
findings.headline: Visitor Levy funding of £108m committed to housing, culture and infrastructure without full detail on outcomes
findings.detail: The council is committing £108m of prudential borrowing backed by the Visitor Levy scheme to fund 472 affordable homes (Fountainbridge, Meadowbank, Coatfield Lane), £63m in City Operations and Infrastructure, and £10.8m in Culture and Heritage projects. This is a significant commitment of the levy to capital borrowing.
findings.matters: Visitor Levy revenues may be volatile post-pandemic; committing them to 50-year debt servicing on capital projects creates a long-term revenue obligation if visitor numbers decline.
findings.figures: £108m prudential borrowing supported by Visitor Levy; £34.1m housing investment; £63.1m City Operations; £10.8m Culture and Heritage
findings.quote: Additionally, Prudential Borrowing £108.0m supported by the Visitor Levy is proposed for the investment outlined in section 4.14.2

findings.paper_title: Item 4.1(d) - Capital Budget 2026-2036 - referral from the Finance and Resources Committee - Appendix
findings.headline: Only £29m contingency in capital programme as buffer for unforeseen costs
findings.detail: The general fund capital programme of £1.7bn has only £29m (1.7%) set aside as contingency for health and safety works or essential unforeseen needs. The document also assumes 10% slippage of budgets into future years, which is built into the plan but not available for new investment.
findings.matters: A low contingency budget leaves little protection if any capital projects encounter cost overruns, which is common in education and infrastructure delivery. Cost inflation will need to be met by reductions in scope or further borrowing.
findings.figures: General contingency £29m; slippage adjustment -£12.1m; as percentage of £341.2m year 1 spend = 8.5% buffer only when combined
findings.quote: A general contingency budget of £29m is included in the capital programme to allow for unexpected or essential works that may arise such as for health and safety, and to assume full use of General Capital Grant in later years.

findings.paper_title: Item 4.1(d) - Capital Budget 2026-2036 - referral from the Finance and Resources Committee - Appendix
findings.headline: Interest rate exposure of £2.99bn on 50-year borrowing at assumed 5.25% rate
findings.detail: The council is planning to borrow £1.58bn of principal to be repaid over 50 years. At the assumed interest rate of 5.25%, this will cost £2.99bn in interest, for a total cost of £4.58bn (average £91.5m per year). If interest rates rise above 5.25%, the revenue impact will be material.
findings.matters: A 1% rise in interest rates would add approximately £15-20m per year to the council's revenue costs once the borrowing is drawn. The council's revenue budget has limited headroom to absorb rate shocks.
findings.figures: Assumed loans fund interest rate 5.25%; principal £1,582.4m; interest £2,992.8m; total cost £4,575.3m; average annual repayment £91.5m over 50 years
findings.quote: The loans charges associated with the advances set out in this report amount to a principal repayment of £1,582.4m and interest of £2,992.8m. This would be a total cost of £4,575.3m with an average annual repayment of £91.5m over 50 years, under the revised Loans Fund Policy proposals, based on an assumed loans fund interest rate of 5.25%.

findings.paper_title: Item 4.1(d) - Capital Budget 2026-2036 - referral from the Finance and Resources Committee - Appendix
findings.headline: £6.5bn of unfunded capital priorities identified, including £2.9bn for North-South Tram
findings.detail: The council has documented £6.5bn of capital investment it wants to make but cannot currently fund. This includes a North-South Tram at £2.9bn, Heat Network Delivery at £1.6bn, and Building Improvements at £379m. These projects are deferred pending additional funding sources.
findings.matters: A large backlog of unfunded priorities signals either that the council's capital ambitions exceed its revenue capacity to service debt, or that it expects external funding (Scottish Government, UK Government, developer contributions) that may not materialise.
findings.figures: £6.5bn total unfunded priorities; North-South Tram £2,900m; Heat Network Delivery £1,635.4m; Building Improvement Programme £378.9m
findings.quote: An updated profile of unfunded capital priorities, considered in the Capital Budget Update 2026-36 report to Finance and Resources Committee on 18th November 23025, is provided in Appendix 4. This details the capital investment required to deliver on Council commitments and totals £6.5bn.

findings.paper_title: Item 4.1(d) - Capital Budget 2026-2036 - referral from the Finance and Resources Committee - Appendix
findings.headline: HRA debt servicing ratio reaches 67% of revenue by 2030/31, the highest in the plan period
findings.detail: The proportion of Housing Revenue Account revenue needed to cover debt servicing is projected to grow from 38.6% in 2025/26 to 67.1% by 2030/31. This is driven by the capital programme in the HRA, which includes 2,300 settled homes and infrastructure alongside the general fund's 2,500 temporary accommodation homes.
findings.matters: A HRA debt servicing ratio above 60% leaves little room for maintenance, re-lets, or respond to void rates; it also constrains the council's ability to invest further or absorb housing market shocks.
findings.quote: Housing Revenue Account (HRA) 38.6% 38.6% 40.2% 51.3% 62.2% 67.1%

findings.paper_title: Item 4.1(d) - Capital Budget 2026-2036 - referral from the Finance and Resources Committee - Appendix
findings.headline: Capital Financing Requirement more than doubling in five years, reaching £5.5bn by 2029/30
findings.detail: The council's total debt outstanding (CFR) is projected to grow from £2.8bn in 2025/26 to £5.5bn by 2029/30, an 94% increase in five years. This includes general services debt rising from £2.1bn to £3.2bn and HRA debt rising from £624m to £2.1bn.
findings.matters: Rapid debt growth constrains future borrowing capacity and revenue flexibility; a lender needs to understand whether the council has headroom on its prudential limits.
findings.quote: The ambitious capital programme, including the significant intervention to address the Housing Emergency, has resulted in progressive year on year increases in the Capital Financing Requirement, more than doubling the Council's debt over five years.

findings.paper_title: Item 4.1(d) - Capital Budget 2026-2036 - referral from the Finance and Resources Committee - Appendix
findings.headline: Loans Fund Policy change freed £236.9m of borrowing capacity, now being deployed
findings.detail: A change to capital repayment periods approved January 2026 has reduced annual debt servicing costs, creating borrowing headroom the council is now using for new investment in high school extensions, affordable housing, and roads.
findings.matters: A policy change rather than new revenue has enabled the expansion; if the council's revenue position deteriorates, this new borrowing may become unaffordable.
findings.figures: £236.9m added to capital programme from loans fund review; includes £85.8m for school extensions, £126.1m for settled affordable housing, £25m for roads
findings.quote: The resultant reduction in annual debt servicing has created capacity to borrow and therefore increase opportunity for investment. As such, £236.9m has been added to the capital programme

findings.paper_title: Item 4.1(d) - Capital Budget 2026-2036 - referral from the Finance and Resources Committee - Appendix
findings.headline: Housing emergency driving £581m additional prudential borrowing commitment
findings.detail: The council is proposing to borrow £581m for acquiring and developing around 2,500 homes for temporary accommodation. This is additional to previously approved borrowing of £52.2m. The council's plan to service this debt relies on achieving savings from the homelessness budget by reducing use of unsuitable and expensive accommodation.
findings.matters: This is a material bet on the council's ability to reduce homelessness costs; if those savings don't materialise, the debt burden will not be covered by the projected revenue benefit.
findings.figures: £581.0m prudential borrowing; around 2,500 homes targeted; additional to £52.2m previously approved
findings.quote: Additional Prudential Borrowing is proposed totalling £581.0m to support additional investment in temporary accommodation, detailed in paragraph 4.14.1.1, funded by savings in the homelessness budget as a result of coming out of unsuitable and expensive accommodation.

findings.paper_title: Item 4.2(a) - Housing Revenue Account Budget Strategy 2026-27 to 2035-36 - referral from the Finance and Resources Committee - Appendix
findings.headline: Rent collection dependent on maintaining net rental income of 95.44% despite rising tenant arrears and collection difficulties
findings.detail: The Business Plan assumes net rental income of 95.44% of gross rental income, accounting for bad debt provisions (2.83%), empty homes (1.07%), and Tenant Hardship Fund allocation. However, the document notes an increase in the number of tenants with higher proportions of overall rent arrears and a Rent Collection Policy review has been undertaken. Tenants citing affordability concerns and difficulty paying rent suggest collection risk.
findings.matters: Any deterioration in collection rates below the 95.44% assumption will directly impact reserves and funding for the capital programme. The trend showing rising arrears among a subset of tenants is a leading indicator of potential income volatility.
findings.figures: 95.44% net rental income assumption; 2.83% bad debt provision; 45% of tenants finding it more difficult to pay
findings.quote: The bad debt provision assumed in the Business Plan for 2026/27 is higher than that of 2025/26 due to current trends showing an increase in the number of tenants having a higher proportion of overall rent arrears.

findings.paper_title: Item 4.2(a) - Housing Revenue Account Budget Strategy 2026-27 to 2035-36 - referral from the Finance and Resources Committee - Appendix
findings.headline: Critical dependency on Edinburgh Living purchasing homes from HRA; if this doesn't occur, significant financial risk
findings.detail: The Business Plan assumes Edinburgh Living (the council's LLP) will purchase completed homes from the HRA for mid-market rented use. The document explicitly states that 'Other key assumptions in relation to Edinburgh Living being able to purchase completed homes from the HRA for mid-market rented use and interest rates for future borrowing have also had a significant impact to the Business Plan. Should these assumptions not materialise, it poses significant risks to the financial sustainability of the HRA.'
findings.matters: The Edinburgh Living assumption is not guaranteed and represents execution risk. If the LLP cannot or does not purchase homes as planned, the HRA will be left holding additional stock or unable to deliver the projected financial returns, directly threatening reserve maintenance and forcing corrective action.
findings.figures: c.580 mid-market homes dependent on Edinburgh Living purchases
findings.quote: Should these assumptions not materialise, it poses significant risks to the financial sustainability of the HRA, requiring corrective action to reduce future expenditure and/or increase income.

findings.paper_title: Item 4.2(a) - Housing Revenue Account Budget Strategy 2026-27 to 2035-36 - referral from the Finance and Resources Committee - Appendix
findings.headline: Capital investment programme doubled from previous plan, now £2,879m, creating borrowing dependency
findings.detail: The ten-year capital investment programme has increased from £2,267m (reported December 2025) to £2,879m—an addition of approximately £612m or 27%. This expansion will deliver c.4,600 social rented homes and c.580 mid-market homes. The programme is fully funded by borrowing (after application of government funding and other receipts), with no in-year surpluses or reserves applied to capital investment.
findings.matters: The aggressive expansion of borrowing-dependent capital delivery creates material interest rate exposure. Any increase in borrowing costs above the assumed 5.25% rate will impact reserves and/or require further rent increases or reduced delivery. The document notes that 'risks remain that interest rates may increase and borrowing has to be taken at higher rates than assumed.'
findings.figures: £2,267m to £2,879m increase; 5.25% assumed borrowing rate
findings.quote: The impact of the proposed additional investment in new homes has seen the proposed capital investment programme increase from £2,267m to £2,879m, which will support delivery of an additional c. 2,300 social homes over and above what was reported in December 2025; taking the proposed plan to c. 4,600 social rented homes, c.580 mid-market homes and the continuation of the retrofit programmes in both low- and high-rise blocks. This reflects an increase of approximately 100% in social rented units compared to the draft programme presented in December 2025.

findings.paper_title: Item 4.2(a) - Housing Revenue Account Budget Strategy 2026-27 to 2035-36 - referral from the Finance and Resources Committee - Appendix
findings.headline: General Fund is subsidising the HRA with £38.598m over ten years plus additional housing investment
findings.detail: The council is allocating £38.598m from the General Fund to support the proposed additional investment in new homes over the ten-year period. Beyond the HRA subsidy, the General Fund is providing £581.1m for temporary accommodation purchases and £126.1m to unlock delivery of c.1,100 additional affordable homes. This cross-subsidy was enabled by the Housing (Scotland) Act 2025 which removed the requirement for ministerial consent.
findings.matters: HRA reliance on General Fund subsidies indicates the HRA cannot self-fund its capital ambitions from rental income and borrowing alone. This raises questions about the sustainability of the housing strategy and whether the General Fund has sufficient headroom for this commitment while meeting its own pressures.
findings.figures: £38.598m over ten years; £581.1m temporary accommodation; £126.1m affordable homes
findings.quote: The proposed General Fund and HRA budgets reflect contributions from the General Fund of £38.598m across the ten-year period. In addition, as part of addressing the Housing Emergency as a whole, further General Fund investment of £581.1m to purchase c.2,500 forms of suitable temporary accommodation and £126.1m to unlock the delivery of c.1,100 additional affordable homes, is proposed within the General Fund budget reports.

findings.paper_title: Item 4.2(a) - Housing Revenue Account Budget Strategy 2026-27 to 2035-36 - referral from the Finance and Resources Committee - Appendix
findings.headline: Only 36% of tenants support the 7% rent increase; 52% oppose it
findings.detail: Budget consultation of 796 tenants conducted October-November 2025 found only 36% support a 7% rent increase, while 52% do not support it. Many respondents commented that a 7% increase could cause financial difficulties and had concerns about affordability. A separate finding shows 45% of respondents found it more difficult to pay rent over the last 12 months.
findings.matters: Low tenant support for rent increases suggests political pressure to deviate from the 7% strategy. Coupled with affordability concerns, this creates income collection risk and potential for rent arrears to rise, particularly among the 40.9% of tenants identified as self-payers receiving no government help.
findings.figures: 36% support; 52% oppose; 45% finding it more difficult to pay rent
findings.quote: 36% of the respondents support a 7% rent increase in 2026/27, while just over half (52%) of the respondents do not support the increase. Many respondents commented that a 7% rent increase could cause financial difficulties and had concerns about affordability.

findings.paper_title: Item 4.2(a) - Housing Revenue Account Budget Strategy 2026-27 to 2035-36 - referral from the Finance and Resources Committee - Appendix
findings.headline: Entire capital programme dependent on achieving 7% annual rent increases and key assumptions materialising
findings.detail: The £2,879m capital investment programme assumes rent will increase by 7% per annum until 2033/34. The plan is predicated on this income level. The document states that if assumptions do not materialise—particularly Edinburgh Living purchasing completed homes and interest rates for future borrowing—it 'poses significant risks to the financial sustainability of the HRA, requiring corrective action to reduce future expenditure and/or increase income.'
findings.matters: Deviation from the rent strategy would force either reduced delivery of affordable homes or need for immediate corrective action. This creates execution risk for lenders financing the programme.
findings.figures: 7% per annum rent increase assumption; £2,879m capital programme
findings.quote: Should these assumptions not materialise, it poses significant risks to the financial sustainability of the HRA, requiring corrective action to reduce future expenditure and/or increase income.

findings.paper_title: Item 4.2(a) - Housing Revenue Account Budget Strategy 2026-27 to 2035-36 - referral from the Finance and Resources Committee - Appendix
findings.headline: Reserve balances declining from £59.43m to £25.0m over the ten-year period
findings.detail: The HRA's forecast reserve balance at year ten is reducing significantly due to the proposed additional investment in 2,300 new social homes. The Business Plan maintains a minimum reserve of £25m across all years from year six onwards, with the reserve declining in years 8-10. The document explicitly states this reflects 'a net negative impact on the forecast reserve balance at year ten with forecast reserves reducing from £59.43m to £25.0m.'
findings.matters: A declining and minimum-maintained reserve position indicates the HRA is operationally stressed and has limited capacity to absorb unforeseen costs, interest rate rises, or rental income shortfalls. This increases financial fragility and borrowing risk.
findings.figures: £59.43m to £25.0m; years 6-10 maintained at £25.0m minimum
findings.quote: The changes have a net negative impact on the forecast reserve balance at year ten with forecast reserves reducing from £59.43m to £25.0m.

findings.paper_title: Item 4.1(b) - Revenue Budget 2026-27 – Risks and Reserves - referral from the Finance and Resources Committee - Appendix
findings.headline: ALEO savings assumed in November budget are now not happening in 2026/27
findings.detail: Budget proposals in November assumed £1.0m savings from review of ALEO financing arrangements. Following organisational restructuring of Lothian Buses and Edinburgh Trams and wider ALEO governance changes, consideration of efficiency opportunities is continuing and no saving is now being assumed for 2026/27.
findings.matters: Delay in ALEO efficiency savings signals that these organisations continue to absorb council resources without delivering planned benefits.
findings.figures: £1.0m assumed saving in November, now £0m in 2026/27 budget
findings.quote: The budget proposals for 2026/27 presented to the Finance and Resources Committee on 18 November 2025 assumed savings of £1.0m from a review of ALEO financing arrangements. Given recent changes to the organisational structure of Lothian Buses and Edinburgh Trams and wider revisions to the Council's ALEO governance framework, consideration of the implications of these changes and associated opportunities for efficiencies is continuing and, as such, no saving is now being assumed in 2026/27.

findings.paper_title: Item 4.1(b) - Revenue Budget 2026-27 – Risks and Reserves - referral from the Finance and Resources Committee - Appendix
findings.headline: Demographic investment is being reduced despite continued underlying demand pressure
findings.detail: Demographic provision for growth has been reduced from £3.9m in the 2025/26 baseline to £2.4m in 2026/27 and further to £1.9m in 2027/28, despite recognition that 'more effective demand management, greater use of preventative approaches...and service prioritisation...will likely be required' to make this sustainable.
findings.matters: Population growth pressures (particularly secondary education and adult social care) are recognised but underfunded; this suggests growing structural deficit between demand and resources.
findings.figures: Demographic investment: £3.9m (2025/26 baseline), £2.4m (2026/27), £1.9m (2027/28)
findings.quote: These projections show continuing reductions in the overall pupil roll but with this position masking two offsetting trends, with the primary school sector roll decreasing until 2031 but the (more expensive due to lower pupil:teacher ratios) secondary roll continuing to increase until around 2030...Given the significant incremental funding gaps in future years of the budget framework, more effective demand management, greater use of preventative approaches to service delivery and service prioritisation across the Council will likely be required for this level of funding to prove sustainable over the medium to longer term.

findings.paper_title: Item 4.1(b) - Revenue Budget 2026-27 – Risks and Reserves - referral from the Finance and Resources Committee - Appendix
findings.headline: Failures to accommodate remain at ~250 households per month despite £12.5m investment; housing allocations suspended since April 2025
findings.detail: Housing allocations policy has been suspended since April 2025, meaning fewer households exit temporary accommodation. Despite significant investment in homelessness services, failures to accommodate remain high and unsuitable temporary accommodation continues to be used.
findings.matters: The council's housing strategy is not reducing the emergency; demand remains unmet despite increased spending, suggesting unsustainable cost trajectory.
findings.figures: ~250 households per month in failures to accommodate; £12.5m additional investment in 2025/26
findings.quote: As has been reported extensively elsewhere, demand for temporary accommodation continues to rise and failures to accommodate remain high (at around 250 households per month) along with the continued use of unsuitable temporary accommodation. The suspension of the Council housing allocations policy has been in place since April 2025, meaning that fewer households are moving out of temporary accommodation to a permanent home.

findings.paper_title: Item 4.1(b) - Revenue Budget 2026-27 – Risks and Reserves - referral from the Finance and Resources Committee - Appendix
findings.headline: Edinburgh Integration Joint Board faces a £26.9m savings requirement with £16.0m falling on council-delegated services
findings.detail: EIJB reported in December 2025 that it faces a gross in-year savings requirement of £26.9m for 2026/27, of which £16.0m relates to council-delegated adult social care services. This includes a shortfall in Real Living Wage funding for commissioned care of £1.2m.
findings.matters: Adult social care is the largest demand-driven service; a structural funding gap of this scale signals that the council cannot meet demographic demand within allocated resources.
findings.figures: £26.9m gross savings requirement for EIJB; £16.0m council-delegated; £1.2m Real Living Wage shortfall
findings.quote: An update on the projected EIJB position for 2026/27 was considered by the Board on 16 December 2025. This pointed to a gross in-year savings requirement of £26.9m, with £16.0m of this total relating to Council-delegated services.

findings.paper_title: Item 4.1(b) - Revenue Budget 2026-27 – Risks and Reserves - referral from the Finance and Resources Committee - Appendix
findings.headline: Planned savings proposals have been downgraded by £0.859m in the two months since November announcement
findings.detail: In November, savings totalling £22.9m were presented. Updated progress assessment has now reduced this to £22.041m, reflecting that some proposals were at early stage or subject to dependencies and internal/external factors.
findings.matters: The council's ability to balance the budget rests on delivering savings; deterioration in savings confidence between November and February signals increasing delivery risk.
findings.figures: Reduction of £0.859m from £22.9m to £22.041m
findings.quote: Savings proposals totalling £22.9m were presented to the Finance and Resources Committee on 18 November 2025. Recognising that some of these were, at that point, at a comparatively early stage of development or subject to various internal and external factors and dependencies, an updated progress assessment has now been undertaken as shown in the Medium-Term Financial Plan report elsewhere on this agenda. This process has resulted in an overall assumed reduction in the level of savings delivery of £0.859m to £22.041m.

findings.paper_title: Item 4.1(b) - Revenue Budget 2026-27 – Risks and Reserves - referral from the Finance and Resources Committee - Appendix
findings.headline: One-quarter of approved savings are not materialising through their intended routes and £5.9m in persistent shortfalls are being absorbed into risk contingency
findings.detail: Month seven monitoring shows 26% of approved savings (£11.3m total) not anticipated to deliver sustainably. This includes £5.9m of recurring shortfalls in financial strategy, parking income and property rationalisation now being covered from the risk contingency buffer.
findings.matters: Structural savings are failing to materialise; the council is relying on one-off contingency rather than permanent spending reductions, which erodes budget flexibility in future years.
findings.figures: £11.3m of £43m approved savings not delivering sustainably; £5.9m in recurring shortfalls
findings.quote: The current year's revenue monitoring does, however, indicate that around 26% of approved savings or assumed management of pressures are not currently anticipated to be delivered through the intended means and/or on a sustainable basis. This total of £11.3m comprises a combination of: (i) savings where delivery is anticipated in subsequent years... (ii) pressures in repairs and maintenance... and (iii) a number of other assumed-recurring shortfalls. This last category, totalling £5.9m across the main areas of Financial Strategy and Best Value, parking income and property rationalisation, is proposed to be addressed in 2026/27 primarily through application against £5m of the budget framework's risk contingency.

findings.paper_title: Item 4.1(b) - Revenue Budget 2026-27 – Risks and Reserves - referral from the Finance and Resources Committee - Appendix
findings.headline: Edinburgh Leisure required £1.868m emergency funding injection in December 2025 and is banking on transformation gains it has not yet delivered
findings.detail: Council approved additional service payment to maintain EL's financial stability pending delivery of transformation programme. The 2026/27 budget assumes no additional payment and that EL's transformation will fully mitigate budget pressure, but this is not yet demonstrated.
findings.matters: A significant arm's-length organisation continues to need emergency support; if transformation fails to deliver, further calls on the council are likely.
findings.figures: £1.868m additional payment December 2025; core service payment £8.0m baseline assumed for 2026/27
findings.quote: At the meeting of Council on 18 December 2025, members approved the provision of an additional in-year service payment of £1.868m to maintain EL's financial stability and service continuity, pending the realisation of full transformation programme benefits in future years.

findings.paper_title: Item 4.1(b) - Revenue Budget 2026-27 – Risks and Reserves - referral from the Finance and Resources Committee - Appendix
findings.headline: Parking income is falling short by 3 percentage points and the gap appears structural
findings.detail: The 2025/26 budget assumed a 7% net increase in parking revenue following 10% charge rises, but actual income growth since April 2025 has been only 4%. Officers have concluded this is likely recurring and have allocated the shortfall against risk contingency.
findings.matters: Parking income is a material revenue source; if the shortfall persists it will require either additional service cuts or reserve draws in future years.
findings.figures: 7% assumed net increase, 4% actual increase achieved; 10% charge rise approved for 2025/26
findings.quote: Since April 2025, however, the average increase in additional income generated has only been around 4%. While officers have considered a range of measures to address this shortfall, on the basis that it is likely to be recurring in nature, this shortfall has been allocated against the risk contingency contained within the budget framework.

findings.paper_title: Item 7.4 - Loans Fund Review - referral from the Finance and Resources Committee - Appendix
findings.headline: Extended repayment extends absolute interest costs, but council argues shorter periods would force service cuts or infrastructure underinvestment
findings.detail: While the risk section acknowledges that cumulative interest over 50 years could exceed 30 years (though NPV-positive due to time value of money), the council argues the current policy 'could potentially harm the financial sustainability of the Council if it means that service cuts or underinvestment in infrastructure renewal are needed to balance the budget.' This suggests the council views the headroom as necessary to avoid cuts.
findings.matters: This reveals budget pressure: the council is implying it cannot balance its medium-term budget without either extending debt repayment or cutting services. The policy trades future interest costs for near-term flexibility—a decision that affects long-term financial resilience.
findings.figures: No specific additional interest cost figures disclosed; NPV benefit of £90m is present-value positive but absolute interest costs increase over 50-year term.
findings.quote: The current policy could potentially harm the financial sustainability of the Council if it means that service cuts or underinvestment in infrastructure renewal are needed to balance the budget.

findings.paper_title: Item 7.4 - Loans Fund Review - referral from the Finance and Resources Committee - Appendix
findings.headline: Audit Scotland Best Value report identified debt levels as a concern, prompting this policy shift
findings.detail: The Section 95 officer undertook this review following Audit Scotland's Best Value report, which specifically referenced the council's levels of debt. The council's MTFP identified a 'need for short-term budget flexibility' that this policy change is designed to provide by reducing near-term debt servicing requirements.
findings.matters: External audit criticism of debt levels signals underlying financial stress. This policy change is reactive to audit findings rather than proactive optimization, suggesting the council was previously unable to balance its budget without extending repayment periods.
findings.figures: Council states audit flagged debt levels; no specific debt-to-revenue ratios provided in this document.
findings.quote: As part of the implementation of the Budget Strategy and following Audit Scotland's Best Value report on the Council, which referenced the Council's levels of debt, the Section 95 officer has undertaken a review of the Council's policies and strategy towards borrowing.

findings.paper_title: Item 7.4 - Loans Fund Review - referral from the Finance and Resources Committee - Appendix
findings.headline: Council extends debt repayment periods from 30 to 50 years, creating significant annual budget headroom but longer total debt maturity
findings.detail: From 2026/27, General Fund buildings move from 30-year equal instalment to 50-year annuity repayment; HRA new homes extend from 30 to 50 years. This reduces annual loans charges, creating £45m headroom in General Fund 2026/27 declining to £30m by 2030/31, and £6m-£17m in HRA. The change has a positive net present value of £90m, but will accumulate higher total interest costs over the extended period.
findings.matters: This is a material restructuring of the council's debt profile, extending the maturity of borrowings and shifting costs across generations. Lenders must understand whether this improves or masks underlying financial sustainability, and how the freed headroom will be deployed.
findings.figures: General Fund loans charges proposed at £103m (2026/27) rising to £146m (2030/31); £45m headroom in 2026/27. HRA charges £55m-£146m over the decade. Net present value benefit of £90m.
findings.quote: From 2026/27, officers propose: General Fund (buildings and other long-life assets): move from a 30-year EIP to a 50-year annuity method.

findings.paper_title: Item 7.5 - Treasury Management Mid-Year Report 2025-26 - referral from the Finance and Resources Committee
findings.headline: Treasury cash fund delivered strong returns of 4.29% annualized, outperforming benchmark and generating additional income to offset borrowing costs.
findings.detail: Pooled cash fund managed with Lothian Pension Fund returned 4.29% over H1 2025-26 vs 4.14% benchmark, delivering 15 basis points outperformance. Fund held 40%+ in Money Market Funds for liquidity, 33% in UK Government DMADF, and 20% in loans to other local authorities, maintaining security while optimizing returns.
findings.matters: Strong treasury returns provide material income to help offset the rising cost of the council's substantial new borrowing in a high interest rate environment
findings.figures: 4.29% actual return vs 4.14% benchmark; 15 basis points outperformance
findings.quote: The Cash Fund returned an annualised 4.29% over the six months against a benchmark of 4.14%.

findings.paper_title: Item 7.5 - Treasury Management Mid-Year Report 2025-26 - referral from the Finance and Resources Committee
findings.headline: The council has £1.05 billion in committed borrowing through 2027/28 locked in at 20+ year high interest rates despite Bank Rate cuts.
findings.detail: Council borrowed £155m in H1 2025-26 and requires £189m more in H2, then £451m in 2026/27 and £411m in 2027/28. Despite five Bank Rate cuts from 4.5% to 4.0%, PWLB medium and long-term rates have risen to 20+ year highs. Officers describe this as creating 'substantial interest rate risk' that constrains future financing options.
findings.matters: Multi-year commitment to elevated interest rates directly impacts loan charges, financial sustainability, and limits flexibility to manage debt costs
findings.figures: £189m H2 2025-26, £451m 2026-27, £411m 2027-28; PWLB rates at 20+ year highs; 10-year gilt range 4.45-4.82%, 20-year gilt range 5.10-5.55%
findings.quote: the Council still has a substantial interest rate risk. To meet the in-year borrowing requirement, a further £189m needs to be borrowed in the second half of the year with a further £451m in 2026/27 and £411m in 2027/28.

findings.paper_title: Item 7.6 - Treasury Management Annual Report 2024-25 - referral from the Finance and Resources Committee
findings.headline: Council exploring alternative funding sources including local climate bonds and National Wealth Fund financing
findings.detail: Officers are investigating the feasibility of issuing local climate bonds (structured as Peer to Peer lending) and are in detailed discussions with the National Wealth Fund for financing the Waterfront Regeneration project at PWLB Infrastructure Rate. These represent a diversification away from the council's traditional PWLB borrowing.
findings.matters: Exploration of alternative funding sources can indicate either prudent diversification to manage refinancing risk, or a search for better terms due to cost pressures on traditional PWLB borrowing. The Waterfront project represents a significant capital commitment requiring dedicated long-term financing.
findings.figures: Investigating local climate bonds; National Wealth Fund financing at PWLB Infrastructure Rate for Waterfront Regeneration project
findings.quote: Officers have also been in detailed discussion with the National Wealth Fund over the provision of finance for the Waterfront Regeneration project.

findings.paper_title: Item 7.6 - Treasury Management Annual Report 2024-25 - referral from the Finance and Resources Committee
findings.headline: External interest costs increased 14% year-on-year to £67.2m due to higher rates and £290m new borrowing
findings.detail: The council's total debt servicing cost rose from £74.3m in 2023/24 to £77.63m in 2024/25. External interest specifically jumped from £58.8m to £67.2m (an increase of £8.4m), reflecting both the full-year impact of prior borrowing taken at elevated rates and £290m of new borrowing undertaken at an average weighted rate of 4.47% during 2024/25.
findings.matters: A 14% year-on-year increase in external interest costs is material and directly constrains the council's revenue budget, reducing financial flexibility for service delivery and future borrowing capacity.
findings.figures: External interest £67.2m (2024/25) vs £58.8m (2023/24); new borrowing £290m at average 4.47%; total debt cost £77.63m vs £74.3m
findings.quote: The external interest cost component of that increased from £58.8m to £67.2, reflecting the full year cost of the 2023/24 borrowing and the £290m of external borrowing taken during the year.

findings.paper_title: 8.14 - 2024-25 Capital Outturn
findings.headline: Greendykes K&L delayed £6.7m due to sub-contractor and utility issues; Murrayburn Gate delayed £5.0m during contract negotiation
findings.detail: Greendykes K&L suffered a £6.7m delay due to sub-contractor problems compounded by Scottish Power utility delays on a substation connection. Murrayburn Gate was delayed £5.0m while contract agreement was negotiated. These execution challenges indicate variable delivery capability within the housing programme.
findings.matters: Contractor failures and third-party dependencies (especially utilities) on housing delivery create schedule and financial risk. Variable execution suggests potential for future delays on an expanded housing programme.
findings.figures: £6.7m (Greendykes), £5.0m (Murrayburn Gate)
findings.quote: Greendykes K&L suffered a slow start on site (delay of £6.7m) due to issues with a sub-contractor and delays with Scottish Power relating to a substation. Murrayburn Gate started late as the contract took longer than expected to be agreed (delay of £5.0m)

findings.paper_title: 8.14 - 2024-25 Capital Outturn
findings.headline: HRA pausing right-to-buy repurchase disposals indefinitely to boost housing stock, affecting medium-term borrowing and cash flow
findings.detail: The council has paused disposals from its Acquisitions and Disposals programme (£0.8m) to boost total housing stock, with this pause continuing through 2025-26. This deliberate strategic shift will increase both rental income and borrowing costs in the HRA business plan.
findings.matters: A permanent shift in capital allocation strategy has ongoing implications for HRA cash flow, borrowing requirement forecasts, and medium-term financial position. It signals reorientation toward direct housing provision rather than asset recycling.
findings.figures: £0.8m per year
findings.quote: The decision to pause the disposals part of the Acquisitions and Disposals programme (£0.8m) is likely to continue into 2025-26 to boost the housing stock, which will affect the HRA business plan with increased rental income and borrowing costs

findings.paper_title: 8.14 - 2024-25 Capital Outturn
findings.headline: HRA income fell £4.1m short of budget, forcing £10m additional borrowing and increasing debt service by £0.6m
findings.detail: Housing Revenue Account rental and other income undershot budget by £4.1m. Combined with £5.9m expenditure overspend (mainly void property works and improvements), total additional borrowing reached almost £10m, adding £0.6m to loan charges in 2025-26.
findings.matters: Underperformance on income reduces cash generation and forces higher borrowing. Additional debt service tightens the HRA revenue budget and reduces financial flexibility in the coming year.
findings.figures: £4.1m income shortfall, £10m additional borrowing requirement, £0.6m higher loan charges in 2025-26
findings.quote: The HRA has received £4.1m less income than was budgeted. With the expenditure in the programme totalling £5.9m more than budget and receiving £4.1m less income, the Loans Fund Advances requirement was almost £10m more than budget

findings.paper_title: 8.14 - 2024-25 Capital Outturn
findings.headline: Millerhill Heat Offtake blocked by unresolved legal issues for full financial year
findings.detail: A £7.9m energy project did not start in 2024-25 due to legal impediments. While the issues are now resolved, a complete year's delay on a material capital project indicates inadequate risk identification and management during project development.
findings.matters: Legal issues severe enough to halt a project signal underlying complexity and execution risk. Delays on energy transition projects conflict with the council's net-zero 2030 target and carbon reduction commitments.
findings.quote: the Millerhill Heat Offtake unit (£7.9m) which has not started due to legal issues. These have now been resolved, and it is expected to start in 2025-26

findings.paper_title: 8.14 - 2024-25 Capital Outturn
findings.headline: NHS has withdrawn its capital contribution to Liberton High School, forcing council to absorb costs previously shared
findings.detail: The £14.7m delay on the new Liberton High School is driven by both unforeseen site conditions and a loss of funding partner support. The NHS was expected to contribute capital to construction but has now opted to lease space instead, shifting the full capital burden to the council.
findings.matters: A funding partner stepping back from committed capital contribution increases project costs to the council, delays delivery of critical infrastructure, and signals either deterioration in the NHS's financial position or unanticipated project complexity.
findings.figures: £14.7m delay
findings.quote: A delay in construction at the new Liberton High School (£14.7m) due to unforeseen site conditions and the need to mitigate the impact of the NHS now leasing a unit instead of contributing to the construction cost

findings.paper_title: 8.11 - Revenue Monitoring 2024-25 - outturn report
findings.headline: Housing Revenue Account required a £0.4m reserve drawdown instead of planned £2.2m contribution, signalling stress in the HRA business plan
findings.detail: The HRA was £2.6m less favourable than budget, primarily due to additional costs for responsive repairs. This forced a £0.4m drawdown from HRA reserves instead of the planned £2.2m contribution back to reserves, a £2.6m swing from plan. The council notes this will need to be assessed through the 2026/27 budget process.
findings.matters: The HRA is a separate quasi-commercial operation. If it is drawing down reserves rather than contributing to them, it signals either the business plan is unsustainable or maintenance costs are rising faster than anticipated. Both are material for a 30-year asset management strategy.
findings.figures: HRA variance £2.6m unfavourable; drawdown £0.4m instead of planned contribution £2.2m
findings.quote: The HRA revenue outturn was £2.6m less favourable than budget, resulting in a drawdown of £0.4m being required from the HRA reserve compared to a budgeted contribution of £2.2m. The variance related primarily to additional costs for responsive repairs.

findings.paper_title: 8.11 - Revenue Monitoring 2024-25 - outturn report
findings.headline: Education and Early Years services face structural underlying pressures of £8.2m, requiring additional resources to be approved for 2025/26
findings.detail: Education Services overspent by £2.9m, driven by underlying structural pressures of £8.2m in Home-to-School Transport (£4.2m) and Early Years (£4m). These pressures had to be mitigated by one-off timing-related underspends. The council has recognised these as structural by approving additional resources in the 2025/26 budget.
findings.matters: These are not one-off cost spikes but underlying demand or cost drivers that the current budget allocation cannot cover. They recur and require permanent funding solutions, not temporary mitigations.
findings.figures: £8.2m underlying pressures (£4.2m transport; £4m Early Years); final outturn £2.926m overspend
findings.quote: As of month seven, an overall overspend of £5.6m had been projected, primarily reflecting underlying pressures totalling £8.2m in Home-to-School Transport (£4.2m) and Early Years (£4m).

findings.paper_title: 8.11 - Revenue Monitoring 2024-25 - outturn report
findings.headline: General Fund reserves fell by £51.9m in one year, to £301.3m, reflecting heavy drawdowns to balance the budget
findings.detail: The General Fund reduced from £353.2m to £301.3m (a £51.9m reduction). While some of this was planned (£2m was allocated to reinstate the Reform Fund; £10.2m was deliberately reprioritised), the scale of drawdown in a single year reflects the council using reserves to bridge a gap between expenditure and income.
findings.matters: Reserves are a buffer against unexpected cost pressures or income shortfalls. A £51.9m reduction in one year, while not catastrophic at this reserve level, demonstrates the council is drawing down rather than building reserves, which is unsustainable over time.
findings.figures: General Fund reserves: £353.238m (31-Mar-24) to £301.317m (31-Mar-25); reduction of £51.921m
findings.quote: As of 31 March 2025, the General Fund reserves totalled £301.317m, a reduction of £51.921m from the preceding year.

findings.paper_title: 8.11 - Revenue Monitoring 2024-25 - outturn report
findings.headline: Homelessness and temporary accommodation demand 1,028 households higher than budgeted, driving a £4.2m overspend in Place Directorate
findings.detail: Housing and Homelessness Services overspent by £4.2m, primarily because actual demand for temporary accommodation exceeded budget assumptions by 1,028 households. While the outturn improved £4.5m from mid-year forecast, this was only because some households could not be accommodated, not because demand fell.
findings.matters: This is a demand-driven pressure linked to national legislation and policy, meaning it is outside the council's control and likely to recur. Budget forecasting that misses by over 1,000 households in temporary housing is a material planning failure.
findings.figures: 1,028 more households accommodated than budgeted; £4.2m overspend; Place Directorate overspent by £3.936m overall
findings.quote: This overspend was mainly due to greater actual demand for temporary accommodation than had been assumed at the time of budget-setting (with 1,028 more households being accommodated as of March 2025), linked in part to national legislation and policy.

findings.paper_title: 8.11 - Revenue Monitoring 2024-25 - outturn report
findings.headline: Approved savings delivery shortfall: only 84% of £28.5m delivered, with corporate savings measures particularly weak
findings.detail: The council approved £28.5m of savings for 2024/25 but delivered only £23.9m (83.9%), with £4.6m not achieved. Corporate savings were particularly weak: £2m cash interest savings did not materialise; £1.4m procurement and contract savings were deferred; £236k redeployment costs will continue into 2025/26.
findings.matters: Savings shortfalls are a sign that budget plans are optimistic. If the council cannot deliver planned savings, it either needs to cut spending or rely on non-recurring items. This cycle repeats and eventually creates a structural deficit.
findings.figures: £28.473m approved; £23.885m delivered; 83.9% delivery rate; £2m cash interest not realised; £1.4m procurement savings deferred
findings.quote: The approved budget included some £28.5m of savings in 2024/25, of which 84% by value were delivered during the year, in line with the position for 2023/24.

findings.paper_title: 8.11 - Revenue Monitoring 2024-25 - outturn report
findings.headline: Integration Joint Board required £12.1m additional funding from the council just to break even, driven by care at home and residential care overspends
findings.detail: The Edinburgh Integration Joint Board (health and social care) delivered a break-even position only after receiving £12.1m additional funding from the council and £2.4m from NHS Lothian. The underlying overspend was driven by slippage in savings delivery and growth in demand for care at home and residential care services, both typically structural pressures.
findings.matters: Social care is both a significant and growing cost for councils, and it is partially demand-driven and outside the council's direct control. A £12.1m funding call in a single year is a material pressure that suggests the budgeted allocation was insufficient.
findings.figures: £12.1m from Council; £2.4m from NHS Lothian; majority linked to care at home and residential care growth
findings.quote: Achievement of this position was, however, only reached after provision of significant additional funding from the partners, with some £2.4m received from NHS Lothian and £12.1m from the Council. The majority of the overspend in Council-delegated service was linked to slippage in savings programme delivery and growth relative to budget assumptions in care at home and residential care.

findings.paper_title: 8.11 - Revenue Monitoring 2024-25 - outturn report
findings.headline: Directorate overspends of £18.9m covered by corporate savings and one-off mitigations rather than base budget balance
findings.detail: The council reported an overall underspend of £2.719m, but this masked an underlying overspend of £18.936m across all directorates. This was covered primarily through corporate savings, other one-off items, and reprioritisation of reserves. The underspend is not a sign of good budget management but of underlying service pressures being met through temporary measures.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand whether a council's budget balances on recurring income and recurring expenditure. If directorates are structurally overspending and the balance is only achieved through one-offs and reserve drawdowns, this signals future funding stress.
findings.figures: £18.936m directorate overspend; £21.7m net savings from corporate budgets and reserves to achieve overall £2.719m underspend
findings.quote: the audited revenue outturn position for 2024/25 shows an overall underspend of £2.719m; note, however, that this overall position reflected an overspend of £18.9m across Directorates, with the balance met primarily through corporate savings and other one-off mitigations

findings.paper_title: The City of Edinburgh Council – 202425 Annual Audit Report - referral from GRBV to F&R
findings.headline: Significant audit adjustments totalling £105.6 million were required to the balance sheet, indicating accounting control issues.
findings.detail: The audit identified multiple errors requiring material adjustments: PPP liability overstated by £26m, Common Good accounting misclassification, non-current asset categorisation errors of £3m, and IFRS16 lease accounting adjustments of £5.061m. All material adjustments were processed, but the volume and nature indicate accounting control gaps.
findings.matters: For a lender, the requirement for large audit adjustments signals that the council's internal accounting controls require strengthening. While none were fraud, the errors (PPP rent uplift, lease accounting, asset categorisation) relate to complex areas material to financial position.
findings.figures: Total balance sheet adjustments: £105.645 million; key items: £26m PPP restatement, £5.061m IFRS16 adjustment, £3m asset categorisation
findings.quote: All material audit adjustments required to correct the financial statements were processed by the council.

findings.paper_title: The City of Edinburgh Council – 202425 Annual Audit Report - referral from GRBV to F&R
findings.headline: Major HR and payroll system implementation delivered significantly late, creating audit concerns about payroll accuracy.
