findings.detail: The council's Oracle Fusion implementation was split into two phases, both delivered late. Phase 1 (originally due March 2024) was delivered October 2024 — 7 months late. Phase 2 (originally due October 2024) was delivered March 2025 — 5 months late. The finance team had to resolve significant issues with data feeding from payroll into the general ledger.
findings.matters: Major system implementations carry operational risk and cost overruns. Late delivery and data reconciliation problems indicate project governance weakness. While the audit concluded staff costs were not misstated, the tight integration between payroll and ledger means ongoing control risk if the system remains problematic.
findings.figures: Phase 1: scheduled March 2024, delivered October 2024; Phase 2: scheduled October 2024, delivered March 2025
findings.quote: Phase 1 was initially scheduled to complete by end of March 2024 and completed in October 2024. Phase 2 was initially scheduled to complete by October 2024 and after revisions to the project timescales was implemented in March 2025.

findings.paper_title: The City of Edinburgh Council – 202425 Annual Audit Report - referral from GRBV to F&R
findings.headline: Social care payment controls failed to prevent £250,000 in overpayments to providers in the Swift system.
findings.detail: The audit identified multiple cases where the council made payments to care homes and at-home carers without agreed payment plans or contracts confirming the rate was correct. A manual review process introduced in December 2024 found and was recovering approximately £250,000 in overpayments by April 2025. This is a repeat finding from 2023/24, indicating control weakness has persisted.
findings.matters: A material control failure in social care payments — a major council expenditure area — affecting both overpayments (wasted money) and potential underpayments (service quality risk). Persistence of this finding suggests governance issues.
findings.figures: £250,000 in overpayments identified and in recovery; control tightened December 2024 to manual review of non-matching invoices
findings.quote: By April 2025, approximately £250,000 in overpayments had been identified and were in the process of being recovered from providers.

findings.paper_title: The City of Edinburgh Council – 202425 Annual Audit Report - referral from GRBV to F&R
findings.headline: Edinburgh Integration Joint Board required emergency additional funding of £12.1 million during the year, indicating health/social care integration under pressure.
findings.detail: The IJB reported significant budget shortfall during 2024/25, requiring the council to provide £12.1m additional funding plus £2.4m from NHS Lothian. The audit notes this was 'a source of tension' between bodies, and that while there are encouraging signs of improved communication, financial pressures remain significant.
findings.matters: Health and social care demand pressures are structural and difficult to control. An IJB unable to manage its budget within plan signals that council social care commitments carry unbudgeted cost risk.
findings.figures: £12.1 million additional council funding; £47.8 million required savings across Edinburgh IJB with £42.6 million achieved
findings.quote: The council agreed to provide additional funding of £12.1 million to the IJB during 2024/25, alongside a £2.4m further contribution from NHS Lothian, as a budget shortfall deteriorated, and funding for the IJB has been a source of tension between the two bodies.

findings.paper_title: The City of Edinburgh Council – 202425 Annual Audit Report - referral from GRBV to F&R
findings.headline: In 2024/25 the council delivered only 84% of required savings, falling short of the £28.5 million target.
findings.detail: While the council achieved a year-end underspend of £2.719m, this was only by applying additional corporate budget savings and drawing further on reserves. The planned savings delivery rate of 84% means 16% of identified savings (£4.6m) were not achieved.
findings.matters: A consistent shortfall in savings delivery — delivering 84% in 2024/25 and 84% in 2023/24 — indicates structural difficulty meeting savings plans, which threatens ability to balance budgets in coming years when the scale of cuts required will be larger.
findings.figures: 84% of approved savings delivered (£23.9 million of planned £28.5 million); 84% also achieved in 2023/24
findings.quote: The council also reports that 84% of approved savings were delivered during 2024/25 (£23.9 million of the planned £28.5 million).

findings.paper_title: The City of Edinburgh Council – 202425 Annual Audit Report - referral from GRBV to F&R
findings.headline: Medium-term financial plan shows £94.2 million budget gap by 2030, with no demonstrated transformational change to close it.
findings.detail: The council is forecasting a significant multi-year budget gap. The audit explicitly concludes the council is not yet demonstrating transformational change activity needed for longer-term financial sustainability. This is a key audit message and a significant Best Value finding.
findings.matters: An unresolved £94m gap with no transformation plan indicates the council faces severe choices about service cuts, tax rises, or further reserve depletion. Lenders need confidence in a credible plan to address this.
findings.figures: £94.2 million budget gap by 2029/30; medium-term financial plan forecasting this gap
findings.quote: There is a medium term financial plan in place which now forecasts a budget gap of £94.2 million by 2030.

findings.paper_title: The City of Edinburgh Council – 202425 Annual Audit Report - referral from GRBV to F&R
findings.headline: Debt is forecast to reach £3 billion by 2029/30, creating essential need for member understanding of borrowing implications.
findings.detail: The audit explicitly flags the council's high levels of external debt as a key message. This is not routine reporting but a specific audit concern about debt trajectory. The capital borrowing alone is forecast to increase to £2.879 billion by March 2029.
findings.matters: For lenders assessing credit risk, a debt trajectory rising to £3bn with members needing to 'fully understand' implications suggests significant concern about debt serviceability and the council's ability to manage future borrowing costs.
findings.figures: £3 billion by 2029/30; capital borrowing forecast to £2.879 billion by March 2029
findings.quote: The council has high levels of debt which are forecast to reach £3 billion by 2029/30. It is essential that members fully understand the implications of the council's external borrowing levels on future years budgets.

news_drafts.headline: Edinburgh forecasts £8.615m council-wide overspend at month three; levy-funded culture projects face December review
news_drafts.lead:
The City of Edinburgh Council is projecting an overspend of £8.615m across all its services for 2026/27, according to the month-three budget monitoring report (the in-year check of spending against budget) before the Culture and Communities Committee on 8 October. The figure was first reported to the Finance and Resources Committee on 24 September, and the paper says "an overall overspend of £8.615m is projected".

Within the committee's own area, Parks and Greenspaces is forecasting spending of £0.203m more than its £7.706m budget. The paper attributes this to "additional transport charges and the cost of temporary toilet facilities". Both are running costs rather than a rise in demand or a fall in income.

A separate paper on the Edinburgh Visitor Levy Cultural Programming Fund sets out how that money will be managed. The council will carry out an income review in December 2026, comparing the levy revenue actually collected with projections. If income is lower, the paper says, "a review will be undertaken of the remaining planned expenditure of the financial year to determine whether there is the requirement to pause projects or reduce the financial allocation". In the meantime, projects in the first year are being programmed quarterly ahead of that review.
news_drafts.paper_title: 8.2 - Culture and Communities Committee Revenue Budget Monitoring 202627 – Month Three position

news_drafts.headline: Edinburgh repaid £32m of market debt in 2025-26, including two LOBO loans, at par with no penalty
news_drafts.lead:
City of Edinburgh Council repaid £32m of loans from commercial lenders during 2025-26, including two LOBO loans, according to its treasury management annual report for the year, which went to the Finance and Resources Committee on 24 September. A LOBO loan is a bank loan where, on set dates, the lender may propose a higher interest rate and the council may then repay the loan in full instead of accepting it.

On the two loans, the lenders exercised their option to ask for a higher rate. The council used its own option to repay. The report says the council repaid "at par with no penalty", meaning it paid back the amount it had borrowed and no more. Treasury management is how a council borrows, invests its spare cash and manages the risks of both.

The council still has £122.4m of LOBO borrowing outstanding. The loans fall due between 2028 and 2066, and carry interest rates from 4.375% to 5.25%. The same lender options apply to them on their set dates. The papers give no figure for what the council plans to do about them.

news_drafts.headline: Edinburgh Council's debt service bill rises £8.6m to £86.2m on capital borrowing
news_drafts.lead: Edinburgh Council's external interest costs jumped from £67.2m to £77.5m in 2025-26 as it borrowed £350m to fund capital investment at an average rate of 4.60 per cent. The council's total debt servicing bill — the annual cost of paying back loans — rose to £86.2m from £77.6m a year earlier. The pace of borrowing is placing the Housing Revenue Account, the separate account funded by council house rents, under strain: the council's own figures show debt servicing will consume 64.6 per cent of housing rental income by 2030-31, against 39.2 per cent now. The council borrowed at the shorter end of the market — accepting loans that mature sooner — to achieve rates below budget, but this created additional refinancing risk if short-term borrowing rates spike when these loans mature.
news_drafts.paper_title: Item 7.6 - Edinburgh Visitor Levy - New Projects - referral from the Culture and Communtities Committee - Appendix 1
